catalogTitle: בפרשה זו גנוז משה ר' ובחינתו אור הגנוז (שייכות לפורים)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Moshe Rabbeinu's name is hidden in Parshas Tetzaveh not as a punishment but because his self-sacrifice bound him to the 'eighth', the hidden light above nature, which shines out again on Purim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with two levels of Mishkan: a Jew who is himself a sanctuary, and a sanctuary of wood and stone, matching Terumah and Tetzaveh as the seventh and eighth parshiyos of Shovavim. He asks why the Midrash Tanchuma opens Tetzaveh with milah on the eighth day, and why Moshe's name is missing from the parsha. He explains that the world was made with seven lower utterances, while the 'eighth' is above nature: the hidden light, revealed on Pesach, Chanukah, Shabbos lights and at a bris, where Eliyahu comes because of mesiras nefesh, as a story with the Chasam Sofer shows. Yitzchak, born above nature, and Moshe, whose soul is from the hidden light, belong to the eighth. By saying 'erase me', Moshe bound himself to it, so his name is hidden in the eighth parsha. The talmid chacham who seems extinguished is stored the same way. Purim is a flash of that light in darkness; the Rav ends urging bnei Torah to gather together on Purim.

en: There are two levels of sanctuary: a Jew who is himself the dwelling place of the Shechinah, and, after the sin, a sanctuary of wood and stone; Terumah speaks of the second and Tetzaveh of the first.
The world was created with the last seven utterances, so whatever is tied to nature is 'seven'; the 'eighth' is above nature and is the hidden light that Hashem stored away for the tzaddikim.
Milah is above nature, which is why it is on the eighth day and why Eliyahu, who comes through mesiras nefesh, attends every bris.
Moshe Rabbeinu's soul comes from the hidden light, so his life was a series of concealments, and by offering 'erase me' he bound himself to the world of the eighth.
The absence of Moshe's name from Tetzaveh is not a punishment but his greatness: his name is hidden in the eighth parsha, the parsha of the hidden light.
A talmid chacham who gives himself over to Torah seems extinguished in this world, but his light is stored away like the hidden light until the world is fit for it.
Purim is a flash of the hidden light sent down in a time of darkness, which is why Tetzaveh, the parsha of the hidden Moshe, is always read before it.

candidateTopics: seven and eight: nature and above nature

title.en: Two levels of Mishkan: Terumah and Tetzaveh

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute whether the Mishkan was commanded before or after the sin of the calf, and explains that ideally each Jew is himself the sanctuary, while after the sin a sanctuary of wood and stone was needed. Terumah describes the building and Tetzaveh the kohen as the sanctuary, corresponding to the seventh and eighth parshiyos of Shovavim; he also asks why the oil for the menorah is commanded here.

title.en: Milah in the Midrash and Moshe's missing name

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Midrash Tanchuma opens Tetzaveh with the law of milah on the eighth day and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's teaching that a father rejoices though he sheds his child's blood. He then brings the Baal HaTurim that Moshe's name is absent from Tetzaveh because he said 'erase me', and asks how that can be, and why the parsha hints at Chanukah.

title.en: Seven and eight: nature and the hidden light

summary.en: The Rav explains that the lower worlds were made with the last seven utterances, so 'seven' is nature and 'eight' is above it: the hidden light that will be revealed with Moshiach. He shows the eighth at the Exodus, in the eight days of Chanukah, in milah according to the Maharal, and in the Shabbos lights and the seven lamps of the menorah.

title.en: Candles, oil and the hidden light

summary.en: The Rav explains the custom of adding a Shabbos candle for each child through the hidden light, and says the kinor of Moshiach has eight strings. Oil, which rises above every liquid and can be lit, receives the light of the eighth; Chanukah, a time of the eighth, connects to the hidden light from which Moshe received the Torah.

title.en: Eliyahu at the bris and the Chasam Sofer's story

summary.en: The Rav explains that Eliyahu, herald of the redemption, comes to every bris because milah breaks nature, and Pinchas earned this through mesiras nefesh. He tells of a mohel's mishap brought before the Chasam Sofer, where readiness to give up life brought a cure through Eliyahu, and brings the Bnei Yissaschar that a mitzvah done beyond nature draws a salvation beyond nature.

title.en: Yitzchak and milah on the eighth day

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yitzchak, the first to be circumcised on the eighth day, was born entirely above nature. Using Rabbi Shimon's view that the Torah's reasons are expounded, he asks whether a child born on a day of 'eighth', like the first day of Pesach, must still wait eight days, and explains that the Midrash proves from Yitzchak, born on Pesach, that he must; this is why the Midrash fits Tetzaveh.

title.en: Moshe's soul from the hidden light

summary.en: Through Rabbeinu Bechaye and the Bnei Yissaschar the Rav ties Tetzaveh to Chanukah and Moshiach, and explains that Moshe's soul comes from the hidden light. He shows concealment throughout: the hidden Chanukah oil under the kohen gadol's seal, the hidden miracle of Purim, and Moshe hidden as an infant, in Pharaoh's house and in Midyan, born as one who is milah itself.

title.en: 'Erase me': Moshe hidden in the eighth parsha

summary.en: The Rav explains that by saying 'erase me' Moshe overcame the instinct of self-preservation and bound himself to the world of the eighth, so his name was hidden in Tetzaveh, the eighth parsha of the book of redemption, with the eight garments of the kohen gadol and an ending that hints at Purim. The Baal HaTurim's reason is therefore not a punishment but Moshe's greatness.

title.en: The Lubliner's soup and the hidden talmid chacham

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Chozeh of Lublin spilled a plate of soup at his tish and Rabbi Mendel of Rimanov cried out in fear, until the Lubliner revealed it had foiled a decree against the Jews. From the gap between what is seen at the table and what happens above, he explains that a talmid chacham who gives himself to Torah looks extinguished, yet his light is stored like the hidden light.

title.en: Purim: a flash of light, and Purim Katan

summary.en: The Rav explains that Tetzaveh is a preparation for Purim, when the hidden light flashes like lightning in the darkness of exile. He brings the dispute over feasting on Purim Katan and Rabbi Tzadok's explanation that in a leap year Purim of the first Adar is in the heart, and says Purim's hidden aspect can be felt even without its deeds.

title.en: Noach, Shes and Moshe; from Moshe to Mordechai

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yalkut Reuveni's hint in the end of Terumah and the start of Tetzaveh that Moshe carried the souls of Shes and Noach, who survived while others were wiped out and did not pray for their generation. Moshe repaired this with 'erase me', rising from the outer level of seven to the inner level of the eighth, and his self-sacrifice returned in Mordechai, whose salvation came from the king's own palace as Moshe's came from Pharaoh's.

title.en: Gathering together on Purim

summary.en: Closing, the Rav speaks of 'gather all the Jews' and the people of Mordechai, whom he identifies with the bnei Torah, and praises the plan for the yeshivah's young men to celebrate Purim and Shushan Purim together. He says eating and sitting together builds a love that learning together alone does not, and connects it to the unity of Shabbos.

catalogTitle: The Merit of the Righteous Women and their Song (Connection to ט”ו בשבט)

oneLiner.en: Through the Chasam Sofer's explanation of why the righteous women sang only one verse of the Shirah, the Rav shows that Parshas Beshalach is a storehouse of emunah, and ties Shabbos Shirah to Tu B'Shvat and the climb toward Mattan Torah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Shabbos Shirah and the weeks of Shovavim as a time for teshuvah, and brings the Sefer Chareidim that saying the Shirah with kavanah and simcha is a cheap segulah for atonement, like Amen yehei shmei rabba. He then asks why Miriam and the women sang only one verse, and brings the Midrash in which the angels complain that the women sang before them. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that nature serves the tzaddikim, so a miracle for a tzaddik is hardly a miracle; this answers Tosafos' question on the Rashbam about the women and the Megillah. A miracle has two parts, rescue and punishment of the wicked, and the women's verse speaks only of the punishment. He then traces emunah through the whole sedra: the sea, the man, Amalek and Moshe's raised hands. He closes with the Shabbos Shirah customs, Tu B'Shvat as a day of judgment for trees and people, and the climb from Shevat to Shavuos.

en: Following the Sefer Chareidim, the Rav says saying the Shirah with kavanah and simcha is an inexpensive segulah for atonement, and it is good to make it a daily habit.

Nature was created to serve Klal Yisrael and its tzaddikim, so when Hashem changes nature for a tzaddik it is a small miracle, while for one who is not a tzaddik it is a great miracle that demands shirah.

The redemption from Mitzrayim came in the merit of the righteous women, so for them the rescue itself was no miracle; they sang only over the second part of the miracle, the punishment of the Mitzriyim.
Parshas Beshalach, coming before Mattan Torah, is a sequence of lessons in emunah, since emunah is the foundation of the mitzvos.
Amalek is the opposite of emunah: he came when the Yidden had doubts, and Moshe's raised hands restored their emunah.
Tu B'Shvat is a day of judgment for trees, and the Rav says to daven then for a beautiful esrog and that even barren trees, and people, give fruit.
From Tu B'Shvat, the midpoint of the winter months, the year starts climbing upward, with a festive day every two weeks until Shavuos.

title.en: Shabbos Shirah and the weeks of Shovavim

summary.en: The Rav introduces Shabbos Shirah and the Sefer Chareidim on the power of saying the Shirah, then describes the weeks of Shovavim as a time to return to Hashem, with fasts mentioned in the Shulchan Aruch and long uninterrupted learning sessions in many yeshivos.

title.en: Cheap segulos for atonement

summary.en: Using the Chareidim's comparison of expensive medicine with an inexpensive segulah, the Rav explains that teshuvah through fasts is hard, but there are easy segulos for atonement such as answering Amen yehei shmei rabba with kavanah, Shabbos, and saying the Shirah with kavanah and simcha.

title.en: Miriam's one verse and the angels' complaint

summary.en: The Rav asks why Miriam and the women sang only one verse of the Shirah, and brings the Midrash that the angels, who sing every night, objected that the women too sang before them, and Hashem let Miriam answer them. He asks what the angels' complaint and Miriam's answer mean.

title.en: Nature serves the tzaddikim

summary.en: Bringing the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that all of nature exists to serve Klal Yisrael and its tzaddikim, so at creation Hashem stipulated that the sea would split. A miracle for a tzaddik is therefore small, but a miracle for one who does not keep the Torah is a great one, and the greater the miracle the more shirah is due.

title.en: Women and the miracle: Rashbam and Tosafos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that women are obligated in mitzvos of publicizing a miracle because 'they too were in that miracle', the Rashbam that the women were the main cause of the miracle, and Tosafos' question from the word 'too'. With the Chasam Sofer he answers that because the women were tzaddikos, the rescue was no great miracle for them, so they are secondary to it.

title.en: Two parts of a miracle and Miriam's answer

summary.en: The Rav explains that every miracle, at the sea, Purim and Chanukah, has two parts: the rescue of the tzaddikim and the punishment of the wicked, which is not needed to preserve the tzaddikim. The women sang only for the punishment, and so Miriam answered the angels that she sang only the verse about the downfall of Mitzrayim, not the one about the rescue.

title.en: Beshalach as a sequence of emunah

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute of the Rambam and Ramban whether emunah is a mitzvah or the foundation of the mitzvos, and explains that Beshalach builds emunah before Mattan Torah. He traces it through the sedra: the Yidden turning back as Moshe told them, entering the sea before it split, believing in Hashem and Moshe, and the man, where only Dasan and Aviram worried about tomorrow.

title.en: The man, Amalek and the Shabbos Shirah customs

summary.en: The Rav brings that the letters of 'man hu' spell emunah, and asks why the jar of man had to be kept in the Kodesh HaKodashim; Rashi brings that Yirmiyahu showed it to the people who would not learn for fear of their livelihood. He explains Amalek as the opposite of emunah, coming when the Yidden doubted, and Moshe's raised hands as giving them emunah. He ends with the custom of putting out food for the birds and eating kasha on Shabbos Shirah.

title.en: Tu B'Shvat: a judgment for trees and people

summary.en: The Rav notes that Shabbos Shirah falls on or before Tu B'Shvat, the new year for trees, when the trees are judged, and brings that one should daven then for a beautiful esrog and make a borei pri ha'etz. From Rashi on the blessing that the tree of the field will give fruit, he explains that people are compared to trees and asks to daven that even fruitless trees give fruit.

title.en: The climb from Shevat to Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav calls Beshalach a reservoir of emunah to draw from, brings the Zohar that the months are divided between Yaakov and Esav, and explains that from Tu B'Shvat the year climbs upward with a festive day every two weeks up to Shavuos. He closes with a blessing for the great yeshuah.

catalogTitle: הנצחיות של המנורה ושל התורה ושל משה רבינו. (שייכות לפורים קטן)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the menorah, as Torah, belongs to no place or time and burns even in galus, that Moshe Rabbeinu's soul is the hidden light that returns in every generation, and that Purim Katan teaches a Jew to see Hashem even in hiddenness.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the repetition of the menorah parsha in Tetzaveh and in Emor and asks several questions on the wording. Building on the Chasam Sofer, he explains that the menorah is both a part of the whole Mishkan and a mitzvah of its own; as such it stands for Torah, above all the oral Torah, which unlike avodah does not depend on the Mikdash and burns even at night, in galus. The ner maaravi, the pure menorah and the 'kasis' allusion to the destroyed Batei Mikdash all show that Torah is eternal. Moshe's name is absent from Tetzaveh not as a punishment but because his soul is the hidden light, preserved and returning in every generation, as Mordechai, who fights Amalek. The Rav then ties Moshe's wish to intercalate the year to the flaw of the moon, Knesses Yisrael, and explains Purim Katan and why the Jews did not accept Purim as a yom tov.

en: The menorah appears in two parshiyos because it has two aspects: in Tetzaveh it is part of the whole building of the Mishkan, in Emor it is a mitzvah of its own.
The menorah stands for Torah, especially the oral Torah and its chiddushim, which is not bound to the Mikdash and continues even after the churban and in galus.
Moshe Rabbeinu's name is missing from Tetzaveh because his soul is the hidden light, and what is hidden is preserved from loss.
In every generation Moshe's soul is present in a tzaddik, in Mordechai's time as Mordechai, and he stands against Amalek in every generation.
The true leader of a generation is recognized by following the footsteps of the earlier tzaddikim, not by claiming that today is different.
Purim teaches that Hashem is with the Jews even in hiddenness; Purim Katan, the double hiddenness of the first Adar, teaches a Jew to see Hashem's name in everything.

Moshe Rabbeinu's name absent from Tetzaveh
kiddush levana and the flaw of the moon

title.en: Questions on the repeated menorah parsha

summary.en: The Rav notes that the opening of Tetzaveh on the menorah is repeated in Emor and brings Rashi that Tetzaveh speaks of the building of the Mishkan and Emor of the order of lighting. He asks why it is repeated, why its place is given negatively as 'outside the paroches', why the order of the words is reversed, and why the Baal HaTurim's allusion in 'kasis' to the years of the two Batei Mikdash uses a word of crushing.

title.en: The menorah as a mitzvah of its own

summary.en: The Rav asks why the extra words 'the pure menorah', explained in Menachos as coming from a place of purity, appear only in Emor, and suggests that the menorah had to be made first, before the Mishkan. He brings the Chasam Sofer's Chanukah drashos: the menorah is both a part of the whole building and a separate mitzvah, so the Chashmona'im lit it in the courtyard before the Mikdash was fit, and the miracle was publicized.

title.en: Torah does not depend on the Mikdash

summary.en: On this basis the Rav explains the two parshiyos: Tetzaveh speaks of the menorah as part of the building, Emor of its own mitzvah. He contrasts Torah and avodah in Sefer Shemos: avodah is bound to the Mikdash, while Torah is eternal and even flourished after the churban; the luchos and the menorah allude to the written and the oral Torah, and Torah is the soul of Moshe, who is netzach.

title.en: The menorah, the oral Torah and the ner maaravi

summary.en: The Rav explains that the menorah's ornaments are chiddushei Torah, the pilpul given to Moshe, so the menorah has an identity not bound to place and time, and 'outside the paroches' says it belongs even outside. He brings the Gemara that the ner maaravi is testimony that the Shechinah rests in Israel, alluding that Torah burns even after the churban, and notes that avodah was invalid at night.

title.en: A light in the night of galus

summary.en: The Rav explains that the menorah burned through the night, alluding to the chiddushei Torah created in galus, and that after the egel it was commanded at once. The ner maaravi's miracle comes from the hidden light, which is Moshe's soul; Emor adds 'the pure menorah' because Torah does not receive tumah even in galus, 'kasis' hints that the light remains though the Batei Mikdash were destroyed, and the ner maaravi is like the Kosel Maaravi, a place never destroyed.

title.en: Why Moshe's name is hidden in Tetzaveh

summary.en: The Rav brings the Baal HaTurim that Moshe's name is absent from Tetzaveh because he said 'erase me from Your book', and argues that it is rather his honor: Moshe's soul is the hidden light, and hiding something means preserving it, a reward for his readiness to be lost for Israel. He adds that in every generation a tzaddik carries Moshe's soul, sometimes hidden, and one can connect to him even without knowing who he is.

title.en: Mordechai, Amalek and the month of Adar

summary.en: The Rav notes that Tetzaveh falls before Purim and brings the Midrash comparing Mordechai to Moshe: Moshe returns in each generation under other names. Amalek, who wants to erase Israel, is Moshe's opposite, and Moshe, who offered to be erased for Israel, is present in every war with Amalek. He brings the Bnei Yissaschar on the angel appointed over Adar and its blessing, the month in which Moshe blessed Israel before his passing.

title.en: Blessing without conditions; Moshe in every generation

summary.en: From the Baal HaTurim, that a sage's curse comes true even on a condition, the Rav derives that a sage's blessing comes even without one, so in Adar Jews are blessed without being judged, and on Purim the hidden light within every Jew shows beneath the masks. He brings that Moshe's soul was earlier Noach and Shes, hinted in the last word of Terumah and the first of Tetzaveh, and that before one tzaddik's sun sets another's rises.

title.en: How to recognize the true leader

summary.en: On 'an eternal statute for your generations' in Emor, the Rav says that every generation has its Moshe, but there are also impostors, leaders of the erev rav who dress in Moshe's garb. The sign, from 'go out in the footsteps of the sheep', is that the true leader guides Israel in the ways of the earlier tzaddikim and does not bend with the times.

title.en: Moshe's prayer and the flaw of the moon

summary.en: The Rav brings the Megaleh Amukos, one of whose explanations of Moshe's plea to enter Eretz Yisrael is that he wanted to intercalate the year. He explains the kiddush levana prayer to fill the moon's flaw: the moon is Knesses Yisrael, which receives from the sun; it was diminished because of future sins and falls further behind the sun each year, so the end of the year in Adar is a time of hester panim, the time of Esther.

title.en: David and the completion of the moon

summary.en: At kiddush levana one asks that the moon become whole; the Rav explains that David is the aspect of the moon, as in 'and David their king' and 'until David grew great'. Moshe wanted to intercalate the year, which means equalizing the lunar year with the solar year, so that Knesses Yisrael would be equal to the sun and the small light would become great.

title.en: Purim Katan: comforting the moon, seeing Hashem's name

summary.en: In a leap year the first Adar brings a double hiddenness and disappointment, and Jews comfort the moon with a seudah on Purim Katan; the Rav brings the Rema on this and 'a good heart is a constant feast', tied to 'I place Hashem before me constantly'. Just as Hashem's name does not appear in the Megillah yet a brachah is made on it, a Jew must see Hashem's name in history, in the news and in everything that happens to him.

title.en: Why the Jews did not accept Purim as a yom tov

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Esther wanted Purim to be a yom tov but the Jews did not accept it, and asks why. He explains that a yom tov, like Shabbos, is a day on which nothing is lacking and there are no poor, while matanos l'evyonim awaken the sun to give to the moon; the Jews wanted a day that draws blessing even in galus and hiddenness, and this is the true meaning of Purim Katan.

catalogTitle: החילוק בין בגדי אהרן - “לכבוד ולתפארת'” ובגדי אחשורוש - “בהראותו” - לוקסוס

oneLiner.en: The Rav contrasts the garments of Aharon, made 'for honor and for beauty' in Hashem's service, with Achashverosh's display of wealth 'to show off', and from there speaks against the luxury and showing off of his own community, the place of malchus and of the feminine side as the end of galus nears, and the great light of Purim.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the priestly garments, made 'for honor and for beauty' as royal garments, and with the Chasam Sofer's reading of Rashi that the Kohen Gadol never wore them for his own honor. Achashverosh wore those same garments 'to show off the riches of his kingdom', and the Rav asks why he was not punished for this while Belshatzar and he were punished for using the vessels of the Beis Hamikdash. He calls his own community a 'behar'oso' community: houses, rings, weddings and even shuls built to make a name. Bringing a sefer, the Gemara and the Chofetz Chaim, he shows how luxury leads to debt, theft, envy of the nations and a coarse soul, and asks for moderation. He then answers the question through the holiness of malchus, explains that in the sitra achra the feminine side is stronger as Moshiach nears, reads Vashti, Memuchan and Daniel in that light, and closes with the light of Purim and a plea for mercy.

en: The priestly garments are royal garments 'for honor and for beauty', yet the Kohen Gadol wore them only for the honor of Hashem, never for his own honor.
Achashverosh's feast was driven by 'behar'oso', the wish to show off, and the Rav calls the luxury of his own community the same syndrome.
Luxury leads a person step by step into debt, theft and shame, so the Rav asks that each person live moderately, according to who he is and where he lives.
The trait of malchus comes from holiness, which is why even a non-Jewish king must be given honor.
In holiness the masculine side is stronger, in the sitra achra the feminine side is stronger, and as Moshiach nears the feminine side of the sitra achra grows stronger.
The salvation of Purim began with the removal of Vashti, and Esther, who followed Mordechai's word, stands for Knesses Yisrael and the modesty of the Jewish woman.
The light of Purim is beyond understanding, and the Rav asks that it be used with sense and joy of a mitzvah, and by pleading for mercy.

title.en: Royal garments, not worn for his own honor

summary.en: The Rav opens with the priestly garments made 'for honor and for beauty', which the Rambam calls royal garments, and with Rashi's comment that the Kohen Gadol did not wear them for his own honor. He brings the Chasam Sofer's question and answer: the golden garments recalled the sin of the golden calf, so the Kohen Gadol wore them in shame before Hashem.

title.en: Achashverosh in the Kohen Gadol's garments

summary.en: From the Gemara the Rav shows that Achashverosh wore the Kohen Gadol's garments at his feast, and that Belshatzar was killed on the night he used the vessels of the Beis Hamikdash. He asks why Achashverosh was punished at once for the vessels but not for the garments, and explains that the motive of his feast was 'behar'oso', to show off his wealth.

title.en: A 'behar'oso' community

summary.en: The Rav says that 'behar'oso' is the plague of his generation and community: houses, curtains, chandeliers and marble built to outdo the neighbor. He then asks about the Gemara on Achashverosh's beds, whose frames were silver and whose legs were gold, although the legs are the lesser part.

title.en: The Ruzhiner way and the couch

summary.en: The Rav tells of his uncle in Yerushalayim, an upholsterer, and of a great Ruzhiner tzaddik there; he recalls the royal conduct of Ruzhin and the Ropshitzer's words about it. The tzaddik had the back of his couch redone in the same costly material, saying he learned from his father that what one lacks inside one does not show outside.

title.en: Gold where it shows: rings, weddings, shidduchim

summary.en: The Rav explains that Achashverosh made the legs gold because they show, and the frame silver because it is hidden: pure behar'oso. Following the way of the Ba'al Shem Tov's students he speaks through the verse, then points to engagement rings, flowers, photographers and food at weddings, and even shidduchim, as the same race to outdo, from 'behar'oso' at the start of the feast to 'to show' Vashti at its end.

title.en: 'Let us make a name' and Jewish clothing

summary.en: The Rav reads the generation of the Tower, 'let us make ourselves a name', as a shul built to be finer than the next one, unlike building to honor the House of Hashem. He brings the Chasam Sofer that Jews do not boast with clothing: clothes must be clean and neat, but fine dress was for Mordechai before the king, while for the Jews 'light, joy, gladness and honor' means Torah, Yom Tov, milah and tefillin.

title.en: How luxury leads to theft

summary.en: The Rav reads from a sefer (chapter 5) that explains how theft spread: excess spending on clothing and the home, the yetzer hara's push to live above one's real standard until it becomes second nature, then debts and shame. He calls for moderation according to a person and his place, not a rat race, and describes wedding costs in Yerushalayim rising to imitate America, with parents in tears.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's wallpaper and his journey

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chofetz Chaim's saying that a house with fancy wallpaper is papered with pages of Gemara, since the extra hours of work could have gone to learning, and the story of the rich visitor who found almost no furniture in his house. From Shmuel HaRamasi, who took his vessels with him, he draws that one's home is on high, and he warns that Jewish luxury among the nations, as in Germany and Spain, brought envy.

title.en: 'Three things widen the mind' and sparing Jewish money

summary.en: The Rav rejects the use of the Gemara's 'three things widen a person's mind' to justify luxury, bringing the Maharsha that they widen the mind toward worldly pleasure until one becomes like Bilaam. He then brings the rule that the Torah spares Jewish money, and asks why the Kohen Gadol's Yom Kippur garments and vessels were nevertheless so costly, even worth a hundred maneh.

title.en: The holiness of malchus answers the question

summary.en: The Rav answers that the Kohen Gadol is a king and his garments are for the honor of malchus, worn for Hashem and not for himself. Malchus deserves honor even in a non-Jewish king, as Moshe showed Pharaoh, Eliyahu Achav and Esther Achashverosh, because malchus has no counterpart in tumah and comes from holiness. So Achashverosh, a king, did not debase malchus by wearing the priestly garments, but giving the holy vessels to common guests did, and for that he was punished.

title.en: What not to learn from tzaddikim

summary.en: The Rav says that the great leaders of each generation may carry a certain malchus, but simple people cannot imitate it; one must know what to learn from tzaddikim, as the story of the chassid who copied his Rebbe's coffee in tefillin shows. Jews themselves should live as Jews always did, and he brings the Kotzker's saying that the world is the text and the Torah its commentary, which is how the Megillah teaches us to read events.

title.en: Male and female in holiness and in the sitra achra

summary.en: From 'binding his foal to the vine' the Rav explains that in holiness the male is stronger and in the sitra achra the female, as R' Chaim Vital saw in a dream. As Moshiach nears, the feminine side grows stronger; he points to 'ladies first', women's liberation and the call to draft women, which he sees as a danger to the Jewish family, contrary to the first mitzvah of the Torah.

title.en: The Megillah at the end of a galus

summary.en: The Rav says the Megillah is the story of the end of galus Bavel, as ours is the end of galus Edom, and in a side note explains why Daniel, prophet of the redemption, erred in the reckoning. The Megillah opens with the strength of the female side, Queen Vashti; the Samael fleeing to Botzrah means fleeing to his strength, the female side. A Jewish woman is not made a ruler, not because she is second-class, but because she stands for Knesses Yisrael, devoted to Hashem.

title.en: Sun and moon, right above left

summary.en: The Rav says that in the future Hashem will raise Knesses Yisrael to be like an equal, as the sun and moon were first created equal, but in this world the right, chesed, must be above the left, din, as 'Hashem's right hand is exalted'. Shimshon could have been Moshiach and fell through a woman, while Moshiach comes through strengthening the right; the right side comes first in halacha and the male is above the female in nature.

title.en: Vashti's banquet, Memuchan and Daniel

summary.en: The salvation began with Vashti's removal, on the advice of Memuchan, whom the Gemara calls Haman and a Midrash brought by Tosafos calls Daniel. The Rav reads Vashti's 'women's feast' as a convention for raising women, like those of his day, and explains that Daniel, whose lot was 'the end of days', was moser nefesh to daven three times a day toward Yerushalayim for the rebuilding of the Beis Hamikdash.

title.en: Daniel and Haman, Esther and Mordechai

summary.en: The Rav brings the rule that everything has a good side and a bad side, as Kayin was split between the Egyptian Moshe killed and Yisro, and suggests that Haman was Daniel's bad side, so that both readings of Memuchan are true: Daniel's prayer worked through Haman as its instrument to remove Vashti. Esther was lower than Mordechai, and her hiddenness under her husband's greatness is the beauty of the Jewish woman.

title.en: The Megillah is not history; the light of Purim

summary.en: Running late, the Rav turns to Purim: one who reads the Megillah 'backwards', as past history, has not fulfilled his obligation, for it draws down the same salvations today. Purim is beyond grasp and will remain when other festivals pass, so the drinking is like an anesthetic; the Megillah is its Hallel and is read at night. Jews drink and sing praises to Hashem, not like the drunkard who becomes a wild animal.

title.en: Rabbah and R' Zeira; moments of favor

summary.en: The Rav explains the Gemara of Rabbah and R' Zeira at the Purim meal: 'he slaughtered him' means R' Zeira's soul was drawn out by the sweetness of the Torah revealed then. Purim is full of moments of favor when 'whoever stretches out his hand is given', and even a simple Jew can bring down salvation, at the Megillah, at tzedakah, at mishloach manos and at the meal, if he does not waste them in drunkenness; he tells of a tzaddik in Amsterdam whom the queen came to thank.

title.en: Be a nebach: pleading for mercy on Purim

summary.en: The Rav says the light of the Megillah is greater than the light of reading the Torah, and that one must come to Purim knowing he is a nebach and plead for mercy, as R' Yechiel of Gostynin did at the Kotzker's door, and with the Ba'al HaTanya's words on Hashem's great mercy for the Shechinah in galus. He closes with a wish to wipe out Amalek from the world and from our hearts and to merit a joyous Purim.

catalogTitle: שבת - יומא דאורייתא' מצוה כוללת' זיווג של בנ"י' “וקראתה לשבת עונג”

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos is a greater Mikdash than the Mikdash itself, the 'kallah' of the Jewish people, and that this is why building the Mishkan does not override Shabbos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's reading that the word 'ach' teaches that work on the Mishkan does not override Shabbos, and with the Ramban's question that the limiting word stands by Shabbos, not by the Mishkan. He adds a second question: korbanos override Shabbos, so why not the building that makes them possible? Through a Gemara and Rashi about the future Mikdash he explains that all melacha, the Mishkan's included, came only through sin. He then develops the idea of 'kallah': mitzvos that include everything, the Torah, the Mikdash and above all Shabbos, the partner of Knesses Yisrael, through which a Jew receives his extra soul. Shabbos is a Mikdash in time, greater than the Mikdash of place, which is why the smaller Shabbos yields to the greater one, and why Dovid HaMelech, himself the seventh, did not build the Mikdash. He closes with the levels of Shabbos kedushah, stories about the Shabbos table, and a call to feel the oneg of Shabbos.

en: According to the Rav, all melacha in the world, including the work of building the Mishkan, came only because of sin; had there been no sin, Hashem Himself would have built the Mishkan.
The Torah, the Mikdash and Shabbos are each called a 'kallah', because each is the partner that comes from the same root as Knesses Yisrael.
Shabbos is the partner of Knesses Yisrael: every Jew is missing a piece of his soul, and on Shabbos he receives it back as the neshamah yeseirah.
Shabbos is a greater Mikdash than the Mikdash: the Mikdash could be destroyed and Jews remained Jews, but Shabbos is an eternal sign that can never be destroyed.
The Mikdash is the Shabbos of place and Shabbos is the Shabbos of time; the smaller Shabbos must yield to the greater one, which answers the Ramban's question.
On Shabbos every Jewish home becomes a Mishkan and every Jew himself becomes a dwelling for the Shechinah.
The Rav says one must strive to feel the oneg and closeness of Shabbos, and that its kedushah rises from Friday night to Shalosh Seudos.

title.en: The Ramban's question on 'ach'

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that 'ach es Shabsosai' teaches that the work of the Mishkan does not override Shabbos, and the Ramban's question that the limiting word stands by Shabbos and should limit Shabbos. He adds that korbanos override Shabbos, so why not the building needed for them, and begins the Satmar Rav's answer with Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai's takanah.

title.en: Melacha comes only through sin

summary.en: Through Rashi's question on the takanah he shows that the future Mikdash will be built by Hashem Himself, and that without the sin of the Egel the Mishkan would have been too. All melacha comes from sin, and since an aseh that arises through negligence does not override a lav, the work of the Mishkan cannot override Shabbos.

title.en: Two Shabbosos and the private sign

summary.en: The Rav reads the pesukim in this light: had Jews kept two Shabbosos they would have been redeemed and no melacha would be needed. He asks how Shabbos will be recognized when there is no melacha at all, and answers that Shabbos is far more than refraining from work; it is a hidden sign between Hashem and the Jews.

title.en: The puzzling words of the pesukim

summary.en: To answer the Ramban fully, the Rav lists the dikdukim in the pesukim: why 'ledoroseichem' is stressed by Shabbos, why every melacha carries misah, and how the passage of Shabbos leads into 'kechaloso', the Torah given to Moshe like a kallah, and then into the Egel.

title.en: Torah and Mikdash as a kallah

summary.en: The Rav explains that certain all-inclusive mitzvos are called 'kallah', from 'kolel'. Like Chavah, taken from Adam himself, the Torah is a kallah because it and the Jewish souls share one root. The Mikdash too is a kallah: Adam was created from its place, the Mishkan is compared to a modest kallah, and so the sotah's water takes earth from the Mishkan's floor.

title.en: Shabbos, the partner of Knesses Yisrael

summary.en: The highest kallah is Shabbos: the Midrash says Hashem gave Shabbos Knesses Yisrael as its partner. Every Jew lacks a piece of his soul and receives it back on Shabbos as the neshamah yeseirah. Shabbos influences the whole week, like Yerushalayim and like a wife, and while a sinner or an am ha'aretz remains a Jew, without Shabbos he is treated like an idolater.

title.en: Shabbos is itself a Mishkan

summary.en: The Rav explains why the parsha of Shabbos follows the Mishkan: Shabbos is itself a Mishkan, called 'kodesh' like the Mikdash. Moshe merited the Torah as a kallah through Shabbos, the 'yoma d'Oraisa' and 'yoma d'nishmasa'. A talmid chacham lives in Shabbos all week, but on Shabbos every Jew becomes a Mishkan for the Shechinah.

title.en: Ledoroseichem: a dwelling for Shabbos

summary.en: Bringing the Zohar that 'ledorosam' means 'ledirosam', the Rav explains that every Jew must become a dwelling for Shabbos. Through the neshamah yeseirah a Jew attaches himself to Hashem, the goal of all 613 mitzvos, and so one who desecrates Shabbos cuts himself off from that closeness and is liable to death.

title.en: The Shabbos home and the answer to the Ramban

summary.en: On Shabbos the Jewish home holds the vessels of the Mishkan: the candles are the menorah and the challos the lechem hapanim, but mainly the Jew himself becomes a Mishkan. Since the Mikdash was destroyed while Shabbos is eternal, Shabbos is the greater Mikdash; 'ach' therefore limits the smaller Shabbos of place, which must make room for the greater Shabbos of time.

title.en: Stories of the Shabbos table

summary.en: The Rav tells of a rosh yeshivah who had less nachas than his yeshivah's cook because the cook sang zemiros, of a poor chassid who asked for Shabbos in his challah and fish, and of a boy who returned to Yiddishkeit after remembering a Shabbos kiddush in the Bronx. He explains that a home filled with Shabbos is a guarantee for the coming generations.

title.en: Dovid HaMelech, the seventh

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos, the seventh of time, is greater than the Mikdash, the seventh of place, and that Dovid HaMelech is the seventh among the seven tzaddikim and the sweet singer of Israel, since Shabbos is made of song. From the pesukim in Melachim he shows that Dovid did not build the Mikdash because Shabbos was already within his heart.

title.en: The Egel could not touch Shabbos

summary.en: Completing the answer to the Ramban, the Rav calls chillul Shabbos a divorce from Hashem and kareis a 'sefer kerisus'. Shabbos precedes the Egel because the Egel nullified the Mikdash but could not nullify Shabbos. Shabbos is the 'matanah tovah' from Hashem's treasury, a diamond that should keep a Jew awake with joy.

title.en: Rising levels of Shabbos kedushah

summary.en: Shabbos is the 'chemdas yamim'; Yosef Mokir Shabbos found a pearl in his fish because the fish held Shabbos. Like the Kohen Gadol who immerses again on rising in kedushah, Shabbos grows from stage to stage: Friday night needs a full kiddush, the morning only wine, and at Shalosh Seudos the eating itself sanctifies Shabbos, which is why there is no kiddush except where there is a meal.

title.en: Oneg Shabbos and the love of Shabbos

summary.en: The Rav brings Reb Shlomo of Karlin that one who keeps Shabbos without striving to feel it will sit in Gan Eden like a bench, and explains 'vekarasa laShabbos oneg': the oneg is part of Shabbos. Shabbos is the day of love, needing no sin offering since love covers all sins, and the day when all creation sings.

title.en: The poritz's sugar and the true pleasure

summary.en: The Rav says that one who does not yet feel Shabbos should believe in it until he feels it, and tells of a poritz who covered a field with sugar to go sledding in summer, whose pleasure a tzaddik dismissed beside the pleasure of Nishmas on Shabbos morning. He closes asking Hashem to help one prepare all week and feel the sweetness of Shabbos.

catalogTitle: קריעת ים סוף - A Revelation of Hidden Depths

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Krias Yam Suf revealed the hidden world, the alma d'iskasya, and from there he explains shidduchim, hidden Jewish souls, and the future tikkun of Dasan and Aviram at the second splitting of the sea in the days of Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Targum Yonasan that Dasan and Aviram stayed in Mitzrayim, and a midrash that the sea split again for them, and asks why Krias Yam Suf moved them when the ten plagues did not. He brings the Zohar, explained in Torah Ohr, that the splitting exposed the hidden world, the alma d'iskasya. From this he explains why shidduchim are as hard as Krias Yam Suf, why the bas kol cannot name the right match, and why Yonasan ben Uziel is linked to shidduchim. He connects Targum to tardeimah, to geirim and to hidden souls, and shows the same hiddenness in Leah, Esav and Dina, and in Adar and Purim. Finally he explains that the first Krias Yam Suf was premature; the second, in the days of Moshiach, will bring the tikkun of Dasan and Aviram, which also resolves the Ramban's view of the Shirah. He closes with Tu B'Shvat and Yeshayahu's song of the vineyard.

en: Krias Yam Suf exposed the ocean bed, which is a revelation of the alma d'iskasya, the hidden world, both in creation and in Torah.
Shidduchim come from the alma d'iskasya, deeper than the bas kol, which is why a match is as hard as Krias Yam Suf and the bas kol does not know the right one at first.
Targum reaches down into the language of the nations to draw close hidden Jewish souls, the geirim, and Onkelos the convert was the first to make a Targum.
Leah was meant for Esav and tore herself away with her tears, and Purim in Adar is likewise a Yom Tov taken away from Esav's months with tears.
The first Krias Yam Suf came before its time and was incomplete; a second one in the days of Moshiach will bring the full tikkun, even for Dasan and Aviram.
Following the Tiferes Shlomo, no Jewish soul is ever finally rejected; every Jew must return to his root.

the future Krias Yam Suf in the days of Moshiach

title.en: Dasan and Aviram stayed in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Targum Yonasan that the 'Bnei Yisrael' to whom Pharaoh speaks are Dasan and Aviram, who stayed in Mitzrayim, and a midrash that the sea split again for them. He asks why Krias Yam Suf moved them when the plagues did not, and why they survived when others died in the plague of darkness.

title.en: The Ramban's question and the hidden world

summary.en: The Rav brings the dispute of the Ibn Ezra and the Ramban whether 'ki va sus Paroh' is part of the Shirah, and asks why it is written in the Shirah's special layout if it is not. He then brings the Gemara in Megillah about Yonasan ben Uziel and the bas kol, and the Zohar, explained in Torah Ohr, that Krias Yam Suf revealed the alma d'iskasya.

title.en: Shidduchim and Yonasan ben Uziel

summary.en: The Rav explains why shidduchim are as hard as Krias Yam Suf: they come from the hidden world, deeper than the bas kol, which is why it keeps announcing the wrong match. Yonasan ben Uziel, whom the bas kol could not identify, stems from that hidden world, which is why people go to him to pray for shidduchim.

title.en: Targum, tardeimah and the first shidduch

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that Targum equals tardeimah in gematria, and notes that the first shidduch, Chava, came while Adam slept. Targum belongs to hidden Jewish souls among the nations, like Onkelos the convert; shidduchim, too, come from Hashem without a person's hishtadlus.

title.en: Leah and Rachel, hidden and revealed

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that Leah is the hidden world and Rachel the revealed world, and shows it in how each came to Yaakov and where each is buried. He then explains that Targum is mekarev the nidachim, hidden Jewish souls, and that no soul of Klal Yisrael will remain lost.

title.en: Esav's hidden soul and Leah's tears

summary.en: The Rav brings the Heichal HaBrachah that Esav had a very high soul, rooted in David and Moshiach, from which Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Meir came, which is why Yitzchak wanted to bless him. Leah, the hidden world, was meant for Esav and tore herself away with her tears, and so Yaakov was punished for hiding Dina from Esav.

title.en: The months taken from Esav, and Purim

summary.en: The Rav brings that the months were divided between Yaakov and Esav, and Yaakov took Elul and part of Av, and correspondingly Adar and part of Shvat. Purim is a Yom Tov taken away with tears, just as Leah took herself away from Esav with her tears.

title.en: A second Krias Yam Suf in the days of Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings Yeshayahu's prophecy, read on the last day of Pesach, that Hashem will again dry up the sea to gather the remnant of His people. The first splitting came before its time, and the sea split only on seeing Yosef's coffin; Dasan and Aviram, who sinned in Mitzrayim, had no share in Yosef's merit.

title.en: Do Dasan and Aviram have a share in Olam Haba?

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mishnah in Sanhedrin about those without a share in Olam Haba and the Gemara's verses for Korach, and the Or HaChaim that Dasan and Aviram are excluded. The Tiferes Shlomo disagrees, since no Jew is ever rejected; the Rav supports him with a remez and explains that Tehillim's 'rebuke' of the sea was for Dasan and Aviram's second crossing.

title.en: The tikkun of Dasan and Aviram and the end of the Shirah

summary.en: The Rav answers his opening question: Dasan and Aviram were hidden souls, so only Krias Yam Suf, the revelation of the hidden world, stirred them, though not enough for full teshuvah. Their tikkun will come at the second Krias Yam Suf; he reads Yeshayahu's 'she'ar ami', 'yimloch' and 'ki va sus Paroh' as forecasts of it, which answers the Ramban.

title.en: Tu B'Shvat and the song of the vineyard

summary.en: The Rav notes that Tu B'Shvat falls on this Shabbos and brings Yeshayahu's song of the vineyard that yielded bad grapes. Every Jew is Hashem's beloved shoot, and on Tu B'Shvat one asks that our fruits, our children, be good, as on Shabbos Shirah we sing to Hashem and He sings to us.

catalogTitle: לימוד מתרומת הדשן - לשמוח בכל עבודה אפ' הכי קטנה

oneLiner.en: From the law that the kohen's garment must fit him even for the lowly terumas hadeshen, the Rav teaches that a person preparing for his own Shavuos must value and be content with even the smallest avodah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with memories of how a youth-group counselor kept him and his friends committed to Yiddishkeit, then turns to the season. Nissan is the spring of the Jewish people, and the days of Sefirah are a time of growth toward Shavuos; like a plant, a Jew needs conditions to grow, namely kedushah and taharah. Since each sedra carries the theme of its week, almost all of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah is found in the parshiyos read during Sefirah. A young man's yeshiva years are his personal Sefirah: he needs toil, tefillah, siyata dishmaya and holiness, and each person is given his own place. Finally the Rav asks why the Torah states that the garment must fit the kohen only by terumas hadeshen: because a person may feel a simple job does not suit him. One must value small avodah, and even a tree without fruit belongs in shul on Shavuos.

en: Nissan is the spring of the Jewish people, and the days of Sefirah are a time of growth that leads to receiving the Torah on Shavuos.
Just as a plant needs conditions to grow, a Jew needs kedushah and taharah in order to merit his share in the Torah.
Almost all the halachos of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah appear in the parshiyos read during the weeks of Sefirah.
Becoming a talmid chacham requires toil, but also tefillah, siyata dishmaya and guarding one's holiness.
The Torah mentions that the kohen's garment must fit him only by terumas hadeshen, to teach that even the simplest avodah must suit a person.
A truly great person understands the importance of a small avodah, while seeking only the great avodah was the failing of Korach.

title.en: Memories of Zeirei Agudas Yisroel

summary.en: The Rav recalls that nearly fifty years earlier, as a young bochur, he joined a group whose counselor, Rabbi Elimelech, taught them that Yiddishkeit is not mere tradition but the dearest thing a Jew has, worth fighting and paying for. He then notes that the previous speaker already covered the theme he had been given.

title.en: Nissan, the spring of the Jewish people

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Exodus in the month of spring was the birth of the nation, and that the days of Sefirah, like spring, are a time of daily growth until the Torah is received on Shavuos. Like a plant, a Jew needs conditions to grow, and the prayer after counting asks for purity and holiness.

title.en: Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah in the Sefirah parshiyos

summary.en: The Rav brings the tradition that each sedra carries the theme of its week, and shows that nearly all the halachos of the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah, such as forbidden foods, chelev, blood and tumah, are found in the parshiyos read during Sefirah, apart from three he names.

title.en: The yeshiva years as a personal Sefirah

summary.en: The Rav compares a young man's years in yeshiva to his own spring and Sefirah leading to his personal Shavuos. He lists the conditions: diligence and toil, but also tefillah and siyata dishmaya, as the Gemara in Megillah says, and guarding kedushah, with a story of a tzaddik who protected the holiness of his mouth.

title.en: A thousand enter, each finds his place

summary.en: The Rav describes becoming a talmid chacham as the fruit of years of toil, brings that of a thousand who enter only one emerges to teach, and says everyone should still strive for it. Not everyone becomes a fruit tree, but each grows something, and Hashem places each person where his task lies.

title.en: Why 'mido' is written by terumas hadeshen

summary.en: Turning to Parshas Tzav, the Rav asks why the law that the kohen's garment must fit him appears only by terumas hadeshen, though it applies to every avodah. He brings the Gemara in Yoma on how the kohanim raced for this lowly task until a lottery was instituted, and describes the kohen who feels that only an important avodah suits him.

title.en: Small avodah must fit too; Korach's failing

summary.en: The Rav explains that the priestly garments express the kohen's honor, so a kohen may feel lowering the ashes does not fit him; the Torah answers that even here the garment must fit, and if he belittles the avodah it is invalid. He brings the Sfas Emes that this was Moshe's message to Korach: the great person is the one who values small avodah.

title.en: Even a fruitless tree belongs on Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav brings the custom of bringing trees into shul on Shavuos and asks why non-fruit trees are brought. He answers that everything has importance: one who did not become a fruit tree but is content with his portion also has his share in the Torah, and he closes with a blessing to prepare well for Shavuos with joy.

catalogTitle: לטהרנו ולקדשנו - צריכים לשמור על האמונה ע"י שמירה ממאכלות אסורות

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that after the matzah of Pesach plants emunah into a Jew's very body, Parshas Shemini and the days of Sefirah come to guard that emunah by keeping away from forbidden foods, which defile the soul and subjugate a Jew to the forces Hashem took him out of Egypt to escape.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with matzah: unlike tefillin and mezuzah, which surround a person, matzah is taken inside and becomes part of his body, planting emunah. Right after Pesach comes Parshas Shemini, the guarding of that emunah through the laws of forbidden foods. He brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching that those who doubted techiyas hameisim did so because they ate forbidden food, and the law that tefillin must be written only on the skin of a kosher animal. Through the Rambam he shows that the Sefirah sedros hold nearly all of Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah. He then speaks of recent painful events, insisting with the Rambam that they are no coincidence but a call to teshuvah centered on kedushah and kashrus. He urges extra care in kashrus, tells of the Chasam Sofer and of a false shochet, and explains through Rashi and the Midrash that the four impure animals are the four kingdoms: eating forbidden food undoes the freedom of yetzias Mitzrayim, while a kosher table is a mizbeach.

en: Matzah plants emunah more deeply than tefillin and mezuzah because it is eaten and becomes part of the body; Parshas Shemini, read soon after Pesach, guards that emunah through the laws of forbidden foods.
Tefillin, which carry the parshah of yetzias Mitzrayim, the foundation of emunah, may be written only on the skin of an animal that is permitted to be eaten, because forbidden food harms emunah.
The sedros read during Sefirah contain nearly everything in the Rambam's Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah, matching the Sefirah prayer that Hashem purify and sanctify us.
Painful events must not be dismissed as coincidence; following the Rambam, the Rav says they are a call from Heaven to teshuvah, and the recent ones revolve around kedushah and taharah.
Forbidden food leaves a bad nature in a person and his children, so the Rav calls for chumros in kashrus like those of Pesach and for knowing who truly stands behind a hechsher.

The four impure animals named in the Torah correspond to the four kingdoms; eating forbidden food draws a Jew under their dominion and undoes yetzias Mitzrayim, which is why Rashi says the Exodus was worthwhile for this alone.
Kosher food eaten with all its mitzvos makes a Jew part of kedushah, and his table becomes a mizbeach, which is why a full bentching does not ask for the mizbeach as the shorter blessing does.

title.en: Matzah plants emunah, Shemini guards it

summary.en: The Rav explains that matzah, unlike tefillin and mezuzah which surround a person, is taken inside and becomes part of his body, planting emunah. Right after Pesach comes Parshas Shemini with the laws of forbidden foods, which guard that emunah.

title.en: The Ba'al Shem Tov, and tefillin from a kosher animal

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ba'al Shem Tov's teaching, via the Toldos and the Degel Machaneh Ephraim, that people who questioned techiyas hameisim did so because they ate forbidden food. He then explains why tefillin, which teach yetzias Mitzrayim, must be from an animal permitted to be eaten, and discusses Rashi's reasoning for why the skin of a nevelah may be used but not that of an impure species.

title.en: Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah in the Sefirah sedros

summary.en: The Rav reads the Rambam's closing words on forbidden foods, that guarding them brings extra kedushah and taharah to the soul, and ties this to the Sefirah prayer. He shows that nearly all of Sefer Kedushah and Sefer Taharah is read in the Sefirah sedros, except basar bechalav and tumas meis, which belong to Shavuos itself.

title.en: No coincidence: the Rambam on crying out

summary.en: From the Gemara that a person's mazal senses what his mind does not, the Rav says a whole family or group can feel a spirit from Above. He brings the Rambam in Hilchos Taaniyos that calling troubles mere chance is cruelty, and the parshah of 'keri' in Bechukosai.

title.en: Recent events and the call to kedushah

summary.en: The Rav says the recent painful events in their circles revolve around kedushah and taharah, among them an accident involving shochtim; like Nadav and Avihu, each person felt the message was meant for him. He brings a teaching on the shtei halechem and says the trials of food and of the eyes demand constant vigilance.

title.en: Heaven is demanding: signs in the world

summary.en: The Rav says Heaven is demanding more of them, perhaps because great times are coming. He lists an earthquake that killed Jews in Bucharest, a plane disaster, a harsh winter and the passing of tzaddikim, tells how the Chofetz Chaim treated a Mississippi flood as a call to teshuvah, and brings Tehillim that an earthquake signals Divine anger.

title.en: Chumros in kashrus like on Pesach

summary.en: The Rav says Sefirah is a time of teshuvah and that one who wants to merit Torah must be stringent in forbidden foods. Just as Jews keep chumros for chametz, they should for kashrus; he brings the halacha that a nursing mother should avoid forbidden food because it leaves a bad nature in the child, and recalls how the children of the Lower East Side were lost when kashrus was lax.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer, Reb Pinchas Koritzer, and repair

summary.en: The Rav brings a teshuvah of the Chasam Sofer advising not to send an ill child where he would be fed forbidden food, and Reb Pinchas Koritzer's explanation that children fall away because parents ate forbidden food. Then he asks, with the Bnei Yissaschar, how such a youth can repair himself, and answers with heartfelt crying out to Hashem and with the Chasam Sofer's comparison of a Jew to a vessel that can be kashered.

title.en: Rashi, the four animals and the four kingdoms

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi at the end of Shemini that taking Israel out of Egypt was worthwhile just so they would not defile themselves with sheratzim, and Rashi in Kedoshim on being separated from the nations. He brings the Midrash that the four impure animals are the four kingdoms and that the chazir will return the crown, and the teaching that the chazir will become pure, which raises the question of davar sheyesh lo matirin.

title.en: Will the chazir become permitted?

summary.en: The Rav brings the Mordechai on davar sheyesh lo matirin and the question raised by the Acharonim: if the chazir will be permitted, how can it be nullified in a majority. He brings the Chasam Sofer's answers: the Torah never changes, but the animals themselves will gain the signs of purity, or the Midrash refers to the inner root of the chazir.

title.en: The roots of tumah and the Kli Yakar

summary.en: The Rav explains that kedushah can rest on a physical object, as on an esrog or the skin of tefillin, and likewise tumah rests on certain creatures, as the Satan clothed itself in the nachash. The four impure animals are the heads of the kelipos of the four kingdoms, and he brings the Kli Yakar that a sign of purity on an impure animal is worse, like a hypocrite.

title.en: Whom do you trust? The stranger and the hechsher

summary.en: Applying the Kli Yakar, the Rav says a false sign of kashrus can mislead a Jew who would never touch plainly unkosher food. He tells of a stranger in rabbinic dress who was refused a loan of twenty rubles yet trusted as a shochet, and says one must know who stands behind a hechsher, ending with the Rambam's words on forbidden foods.

title.en: Forbidden food undoes yetzias Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav brings that whoever eats from someone becomes subservient to him, as with Esther's feast. Since the four impure animals carry the heads of the four kingdoms, eating forbidden food draws a Jew under their dominion, the opposite of yetzias Mitzrayim, which explains Rashi in Shemini and Rashi in Kedoshim about Nevuchadnetzar and his company.

title.en: The Jewish table as a mizbeach

summary.en: The Rav returns to tefillin: a mitzvah that teaches yetzias Mitzrayim cannot be written on a piece of Mitzrayim. Kosher food, by contrast, makes a Jew part of kedushah; he explains why the short blessing asks for the mizbeach while full bentching does not, since a meal with bread and salt is itself a mizbeach, and closes with a prayer for purity during Sefirah toward Shavuos.

catalogTitle: What the Sea Saw that it Split; Secrets of Music. (ט”ו בשבט)

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the sea split into twelve paths because the redemption from Mitzrayim was only a half, mixing weeping and song like the seven white and five black notes of music, while the future splitting into seven will be pure song.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that had Klal Yisrael said 'Hashem Melech' instead of 'Yimloch', there would have been no further golus, and asks why the sea split into twelve paths while in the future it will split into seven. He brings the Midrash that the sea refused to split until it saw the coffin of Yosef, and explains with the Rama MiPano and the Chida that the redemption from Mitzrayim came early and is only half of the geulah, like Yachatz; Yosef's name hinted that Hashem will redeem a second time, so the sea agreed. On Shabbos Shirah he turns to the inner meaning of music: seven notes, harmony as a shidduch made in Heaven, the sevens of creation, the Shabbos, and David HaMelech. The five black keys are broken notes of sadness, so twelve paths meant weeping and song together, while Moshiach brings seven paths and an eighth string. He closes with Tu B'Shvat as a time of chesed and new Torah.

en: Klal Yisrael said 'Yimloch' rather than 'Melech' at the sea because they felt that the time of the full geulah had not yet come.
The redemption from Mitzrayim came after 210 instead of 400 years and is only the first half of the geulah, as the Chida explains the breaking of the matzah at Yachatz.
The sea refused to split because the true time had not come, and agreed only when Yosef's coffin reminded it that Hashem will redeem a second time.
Music is a shidduch: notes that belong together give pleasure, while sounds that do not fit are noise, and creation itself is harmonious like music.
The seven notes correspond to the seven days of creation and the other sevens Hashem made, each culminating in the seventh: Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael, the Kinneres and David HaMelech.
The seven white keys are complete notes of joy and the five black keys are broken half-notes of sadness, so the twelve paths of the sea were weeping and song together.
When Moshiach comes there will be only joy, the sea will split into seven, and the harp will have an eighth string, a new song the world has never heard.

the future splitting of the sea
