title.en: Yovel as the return to the root

summary.en: The Rav explains that yovel is Olam Haba, the return of each soul to its root, and that the fiftieth year matches Shavuos, the fiftieth day after counting seven weeks. Each Jew's root, he says, is in the Torah.

title.en: The shofar of yovel and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai

summary.en: Yovel is announced with the shofar of freedom, and Lag BaOmer begins the light of Shavuos. The Rav calls Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai a soul of yovel, a joy without churban, tells of the Satmar Rav singing in Meron during the Three Weeks, and explains that every Jew carries a hidden secret that Rabbi Shimon reveals.

title.en: A Rebbe for everyone, like Purim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Beis Aharon that Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai belongs to everyone, even the lowliest, and a mashal of Rebbes who seat only those with a shtreimel, a kapote or a beard, while Rabbi Shimon seats all. Purim is the same: it reveals the hidden worth of every Jew.

title.en: Sold to the root of a stranger's family

summary.en: The Rav reads the parsha's case of a Jew sold 'le'eiker mishpachas ger', which Rashi explains as being sold to avodah zarah itself. He says yovel takes him out, even from the ends of the heavens, and explains the word 'eiker' as the uprooting of avodah zarah while the Jew is rescued.

title.en: The thief, the shifchah and the true family

summary.en: The Rav asks why vidui is written by the thief and answers that every sinner steals Hashem's gifts. A thief fallen further is tied to the klipah of the shifchah and wants to stay a slave, but yovel frees him by force; the word shifchah means attached, and yovel returns him to his true mishpachah.

title.en: Nineteen geulos and Shemoneh Esrei

summary.en: The Rav brings the Baal HaTurim that geulah appears nineteen times in the parsha, against the blessings of Shemoneh Esrei. The twelfth, at 'le'eiker mishpachas ger', matches the blessing against the heretics, and the thirteenth, 'one of his brothers shall redeem him', follows; then he asks what the remedy is for one who has fallen and is not yet redeemed.

title.en: Good friends redeem: Malachi and a story

summary.en: The Rav's answer is attachment to Torah and good company. He brings Malachi, the last prophet, who speaks to broken hearts and says those who fear Hashem speak to one another, and tells of a chassid saved from sin by the thought of his friends, to whom the Rebbe said good friends can do what geonim cannot. A good brother redeems, the thirteenth blessing, and 'dodo' leads to the fourteenth, David.

title.en: Rus, David and Beis Lechem, place of yovel

summary.en: Shavuos is the day of David and Moshiach, and Rus, redeemed from Moav back to her root, is read then. The Rav brings the Bach's question on David in the blessing of Yerushalayim and answers that David is the essence of Yerushalayim, then shows that Beis Lechem, with Kever Rochel and Yirmiyahu's 'veshavu banim ligvulam', is the place of yovel, covered now by klipah as the holiest places are.

title.en: Lag BaOmer and the secrets of every Jew

summary.en: The Rav returns to Lag BaOmer, when yovel and the soul of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai are felt, and the great joy at Meron. Believing in Rabbi Shimon means believing the Torah has secrets; as the Torah has pshat, remez, drush and sod, so does every Jew, and his hidden secret will be revealed.

catalogTitle: A שבת with a hint of שבועות; Torah- Above Mathematical Calculation

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos Parshas Yisro carries the gift of Matan Torah without preparation, because the Torah stands above the calendar, and that Parshas Yisro, like the Aron in the Kodesh HaKodashim, stands above numbers.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the idea that the reading stirs up the time: each day of the year returns with what happened on it, so Pesach and Purim are relived, not commemorated. The Torah is higher than the calendar, so reading Parshas Yisro brings the light of Shavuos. Yisro, a convert like Rus, carries the power of Shabbos, which Hashem gives without our preparation, while Yom Tov is made by Klal Yisrael and needs Sefirah. The two haftaros show this: Yeshaya's opens with Uziyahu's tzara'as, yet the Torah is given. In the second half the Rav asks why the Masorah counts 72 pesukim in Yisro when he counted 75. He rejects the answer of thirteen pesukim read as ten dibros, and answers that Parshas Yisro holds the Aseres HaDibros like the Aron, whose place is not measured. From here he explains that a dedicated talmid chacham's parnassah defies numbers, and urges every bachur to learn long and well.

en: Every day of the year comes back with what happened on it, so the Yomim Tovim are relived rather than commemorated.
The Torah is the source of the calendar, so reading a parsha brings the bounty of its Yom Tov even on another date.
Shabbos is given by Hashem from above while Yom Tov is set by Klal Yisrael from below, so Shabbos Yisro brings Kabbalas HaTorah without the preparation of Sefirah.
The Masorah counts 72 pesukim in Parshas Yisro although there are 75, because the parsha holding the Aseres HaDibros, like the Aron in the Kodesh HaKodashim, is above numbers.
A talmid chacham who dedicates himself to Torah has parnassah that defies numbers, but only when it comes from true dedication; today every bachur must learn well into his twenties.

title.en: The calendar as a revolving file

summary.en: The Rav explains that the reading stirs up the time: Hashem's calendar turns like a circular card file, and each day comes down with what was inscribed on it. Pesach and Purim are therefore relived each year, not commemorated like the Fourth of July.

title.en: The Torah is above the calendar

summary.en: The Rav explains that the world was created through the Torah, so reading a parsha brings the bounty of its Yom Tov even when the calendar does not. Shabbos Yisro is therefore a landmark Shabbos, a second chance to be mekabel the Torah and become a new person.

title.en: Rus and Yisro; Shabbos and Yom Tov

summary.en: The Rav compares the two times of Kabbalas HaTorah: on Shavuos one reads of Rus, on Shabbos Yisro of Yisro, both converts. Yisro is greater because he carries the power of Shabbos, which Hashem fixes, while Yom Tov depends on Klal Yisrael's sanctifying of the months.

title.en: Shavuos needs Sefirah, Shabbos Yisro does not

summary.en: The Rav asks why, if Matan Torah requires seven weeks of Sefirah and the days of preparation, there is no such preparation before Shabbos Yisro. He answers that it is a gift like Shabbos, and shows it from Yisro himself, who came in the middle of Sefirah and converted without preparation.

title.en: The two haftaros of the Merkavah

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the haftarah of Shavuos, Yechezkel's vision of the Merkavah, with the haftarah of Yisro, Yeshaya's vision, the two sources of the two pesukim of Kedushah. Yeshaya's haftarah opens with Uziyahu's tzara'as, showing that on Shabbos Yisro Hashem gives the Torah even without tahara; the Rav urges listening to the Aseres HaDibros with kavanah.

title.en: The Masorah's count: 72 or 75?

summary.en: The Rav says the Torah's precision shows it is beyond a human mind, and describes the Masorah's count of pesukim at the end of each sedra. For Yisro it gives 72 with the siman Yonadav, a descendant of Yisro, yet the Rav counted 75.

title.en: Thirteen pesukim read as ten dibros

summary.en: The Rav offers an answer: in shul the Aseres HaDibros are read as ten dibros rather than thirteen pesukim, which changes the trop and the sof pasuk. Counting them as ten gives 75 minus 3, and the same thing appears in Va'eschanan.

title.en: A pasuk is not a dibbur

summary.en: The Rav rejects his own answer: a pasuk and a dibbur are different things, as the halacha that an aliyah needs three pesukim shows, so the Masorah cannot count dibros as pesukim, just as one cannot pay apples with oranges. He prepares a deeper answer: the Torah comes from a place where time, space and numbers do not govern.

title.en: The Aron and Parshas Yisro defy measurement

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kodesh HaKodashim, twenty amos by twenty, with ten amos from the Aron to each wall, and the Gemara in Megillah that the place of the Aron is not measured. The Luchos came from Shamayim, and Parshas Yisro holds the Aseres HaDibros like the Aron, so its count of 72 against 75 is beyond numbers.

title.en: Parnassah that defies numbers

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that not only Shevet Levi but anyone who dedicates himself to Hashem has Hashem as his portion. A talmid chacham is the soul of the Aseres HaDibros, so his parnassah, like the manna kept in the Kodesh HaKodashim, defies the arithmetic of income and expenses.

title.en: Know who you are; learn long in yeshiva

summary.en: The Rav asks why some kollel men struggle, and brings the machlokes of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai with the Ba'al Shem Tov's explanation that those who failed imitated without dveikus. Not everyone is Shevet Levi, but today, unlike in the old towns of Europe, every bachur must learn well into his twenties to prepare for a world full of tumah.

catalogTitle: כל א' מישראל הוא אות בספר תורה של הקב"ה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the counting of the Jews in Parshas Bamidbar prepares for Shavuos, because every Jew is a letter in Hashem's Sefer Torah and is counted by name, at his root.

abstract.en: The Rav explains why Parshas Bamidbar is read as the preparation for Shavuos. Every Shavuos is a new kabbalas haTorah, received according to each Jew's preparation, emunah and mesiras nefesh. He asks why Moshe Rabbeinu himself had to count the Jews, and answers with the Ramban that each Jew who came before Moshe and Aharon by name was seen to his root and blessed; this counting recurs on the Shabbos before Shavuos. The 600,000 souls correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Torah, so every Jew is a letter in Hashem's Sefer Torah, counted by name and not by number. The Levi'im, the camp of the Shechinah, are above number like the fiftieth day, so only the firstborn's holiness within them is counted. He ends with preparing one's letter during sefirah and davening for Torah on Shavuos.

en: Parshas Bamidbar is the preparation for Shavuos, and every Shavuos Moshe Rabbeinu speaks anew with each Jew according to his preparation.
Receiving the Torah requires mesiras nefesh, giving over one's will, and emunah that one truly stands now at Har Sinai.
Moshe's counting meant that each Jew came before him by name, was seen to his root and blessed, and this is renewed on the Shabbos before Shavuos.
The 600,000 Jews correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Torah; each Jew is a letter, and if one letter is missing or invalid the whole Sefer Torah is invalid.
Jews are counted by names, not numbers, because a person's name is the root of his soul.
The Levi'im, the camp of the Shechinah, are above number like the fiftieth day of the omer; what is counted in them is only the holiness they took over from the firstborn.
During sefirah each Jew prepares the parchment of his body so that his letter can be written beautifully, and on Shavuos he must daven for Torah.

title.en: Bamidbar and a new Matan Torah each year

summary.en: The Rav opens: Bamidbar is always read before Shavuos as its preparation. From 'Moshe yedaber' in the future tense he explains that every Shavuos Moshe speaks with each Jew, who receives the Torah anew according to his preparation, his emunah in his own holy soul, and the fire he brings.

title.en: The Shabbos before Shavuos and the night's preparations

summary.en: The Rav explains that the Shabbos before Shavuos is the preparation for the Yom Tov, then describes the preparations of the night: staying awake with the Torah, the mikvah on the fiftieth day, the longing in Ahavah Rabbah, and the need for still more preparation right before the reading of the Torah.

title.en: Akdamus, mesiras nefesh and standing at Sinai

summary.en: Akdamus recalls the mesiras nefesh of Klal Yisrael so that each person takes it on himself; the Rav explains mesiras nefesh as giving over one's will. He tells of the Sanzer Rav's son who saw the lightning of Matan Torah in Belz, and teaches that one must believe one stands at Sinai and accept the Torah even for hard times.

title.en: Why Moshe himself counted the Jews

summary.en: The Rav asks why counting the Jews is the preparation for Matan Torah, and why Moshe Rabbeinu had to do it. He answers with the Ramban: each Jew came before Moshe and Aharon by name, and like a tzaddik reading a kvittel Moshe saw his root and future and blessed him.

title.en: Every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings that Shavuos is a greater day of judgment than Rosh Hashanah, for spiritual matters, so the Shabbos before it, when Moshe counts the Jews, decides the year. The count of 600,000 corresponds to the 600,000 letters of the Torah: each Jew is a letter, and one missing or invalid letter invalidates the whole Sefer Torah.

title.en: The degalim and the camps of the Shechinah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash on 'Shuvi shuvi haShulamis': the nations invite Israel to join them, and Israel answers that nothing compares to the 'dance of the camps', the degalim of this parsha. The degalim mirror the four camps of angels around the Kisei HaKavod that came down at Sinai, and the Midrash teaches that the High came down to the low.

title.en: Rabbeinu Bachya on the names of the nesi'im

summary.en: Two groups of angels came down at Sinai, corresponding to the 600,000 of Israel and the 22,000 Levi'im counted in the parsha. The Rav brings Rabbeinu Bachya: the four nesi'im whose names end in 'El' stand second, fifth, eighth and eleventh, together alluding to Hashem's Name, the camp of the Shechinah.

title.en: Why the Levi'im passage interrupts the count

summary.en: The Levi'im are not counted with Israel, and between the two counts the Torah inserts 'I have taken the Levi'im in place of every firstborn'. The Rav asks why this is needed here and why 'Ani Hashem'; he brings the Yismach Moshe that in the future the firstborn will return to the avodah while the Levi'im remain.

title.en: Counted by names, not numbers

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the early sages were called soferim because they counted the letters of the Torah, and explains its worth: Moshe counted 'b'mispar shemos', by names, not as a census of numbers, since a name is the root of a soul and each soul is a letter. From here he explains looking at the letters at hagbah, the worth of an aliyah, and calling a person up by his and his father's name.

title.en: The four camps and the five books

summary.en: The Rav suggests that the four camps correspond to four books of the Chumash, with Vayikra, Toras Kohanim, in the middle as the camp of the Levi'im and the Shechinah. The Jewish camp is a Sefer Torah, so no one may move to another degel. On Shemini Atzeres everyone gets an aliyah; on Shavuos this is done through Moshe's counting in Bamidbar.

title.en: The root above number and time

summary.en: The 600,000 letters are rooted in the 22 letters of the aleph-beis, which correspond to the 22,000 Levi'im, the camp of the Shechinah. A root is above number and time and only Hashem counts it: so the fiftieth day is not counted and Shavuos has no fixed date, and so the Levi'im, the Aron, and Yerushalayim are beyond measure. The Rav then raises a difficulty from Sefer Vayikra.

title.en: Two holinesses in the Levi: his own and the firstborn's

summary.en: The Rav answers that the Levi'im took over the holiness of the firstborn, as a kohen does at pidyon haben, and with the Yismach Moshe he explains that a Levi holds two holinesses: his own, earned at the Golden Calf, which cannot be counted, and the firstborn's, which can. This explains why the Levi'im were counted from one month and why the passage of taking the Levi'im stands between the two counts.

title.en: Why the Torah counts again and again

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Torah counts each tribe, each degel and the total, when simple arithmetic would do. He answers that it is a count of names, and that a gathering of Jews is a new reality, as with three for zimun and ten for a minyan. Hashem learns the Sefer Torah of Klal Yisrael, and every Jew is counted with his mission.

title.en: Sefirah prepares the parchment

summary.en: The Rav explains that sefirah prepares each Jew's body like the parchment on which his letter is written. Even in galus the Shechinah travels with the camps. With 'the day of His wedding', which the Mishnah reads as Matan Torah, he describes Hashem's affection for Klal Yisrael and the adorning of the Torah, and says each Jew must make his letter beautiful, for his small letter can make the whole Torah pasul.

title.en: Renewal on Shavuos and davening for Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings the Kedushas Levi that the eagle sheds its old feathers and grows new ones, and so on Shavuos, the day of first fruits, a Jew casts off the old and renews himself; each Jew is the 'new offering' to Hashem. He stresses that one must also beg Hashem to merit Torah and its depth.

title.en: Why the Jews overslept, and the oath of Shavuos

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the Jews overslept on the morning of Matan Torah, and explains they wanted to rest so as to daven with a clear mind, yet one cannot rely on one's own preparation. One must prepare all of sefirah and still rely on Hashem. Shavuos is an oath binding Israel and Hashem; he closes with saying Tehillim and davening for Torah.

catalogTitle: “איש על דגלו באותות” - לפי שורשו בתורה

oneLiner.en: From the camps of the degalim the Rav shows how a good neighbor shapes generations, how each Jew is a letter in the Torah, and how Moshe Rabbeinu, himself a 'mo'ed', gave Klal Yisroel the inner grasp of Shabbos, the Yomim Tovim and Kabbalas HaTorah on Shavuos.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Rashi's two rules about the camps: Reuven, neighbors of Korach, were drawn into his dispute, while Yissachar, neighbors of Moshe, later had two hundred heads of Sanhedrin, centuries after the desert, when Jews were busy working the land. He concludes that choosing to live near talmidei chachamim bears fruit for generations, and adds the Chofetz Chaim's lesson about why he was a kohen. He then explains 'ish al diglo be'osos': each Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah. Through Sefer Yetzirah's triad of time, place and soul he shows that Shabbos and the moadim, the Mishkan and the talmid chacham are all 'mo'ed', and that Moshe, the chief of them, camped before the Ohel Mo'ed and especially taught the moadim. Moshe's separation from his wife shows the Torah as his eishes chayil; this leads to his added day before Matan Torah and to how to prepare for and daven on Shavuos.

en: Rashi's rule 'good for the tzaddik, good for his neighbor' is shown in Yissachar, Moshe's neighbors, who centuries later still produced two hundred heads of Sanhedrin.
The Rav says one must be ready to give up conveniences to live among talmidei chachamim and tzaddikim, because it affects one's children's children.
Each Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah, and the degalim were arranged by those letters, 'ish al diglo be'osos'.
Everything in the world exists in time, place and soul: Yom Kippur, the Kodesh HaKodashim and the Kohen Gadol are the holiest of each, and talmidei chachamim are the 'Shabbos' among souls.
Moshe Rabbeinu, himself a 'mo'ed', camped before the Ohel Mo'ed and gave Klal Yisroel a special inner grasp of Shabbos and the moadim, his own portion of the Torah.
Moshe separated from his wife because the Torah itself was his eishes chayil; with his added day before Matan Torah he raised all of Israel toward that level.
The main thing of Shavuos is the davening, the reading of the Aseres HaDibros and Mussaf of the day; staying up at night must not leave a person too tired for them.

title.en: Neighbors of Korach, neighbors of Moshe

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Reuven, camped beside Korach's family, joined his dispute, while Yissachar beside Moshe produced two hundred heads of Sanhedrin. He asks why Yissachar's two hundred are praised when Reuven had two hundred and fifty, and notes the verse about Yissachar comes from Divrei HaYamim, written centuries later.

title.en: A good neighbor bears fruit for generations

summary.en: The Rav answers that Reuven's leaders were in the desert, where all of Israel learned Torah, while Yissachar's came centuries later in Eretz Yisroel when Jews worked the land. He concludes that choosing a neighborhood of talmidei chachamim shows in one's descendants, tells the Chofetz Chaim's answer to a man who could not have mesiras nefesh, and urges his listeners to remember this when they settle.

title.en: Each Jew a letter: the degalim

summary.en: The Rav explains 'ish al diglo be'osos': each Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah, and Moshe arranged the camps around the Mishkan like the letters of the five Chumashim. He then opens the verse 'Vayedaber Moshe es mo'adei Hashem', which the Gemara reads as Moshe instituting the study of each Yom Tov in its time, and says each Yom Tov has its own flavor.

title.en: The strength each Yom Tov gives

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that there can be no months and Yomim Tovim without Jews in Eretz Yisroel, and calls it a chessed that Jews always remained there, since each Yom Tov gives the nation a strength to live on all year. He describes how the Satmar Rav's face looked different on each Yom Tov, and explains that Moshe gave Israel the inner understanding of each Yom Tov.

title.en: Time, place and soul: the talmid chacham as Shabbos

summary.en: Citing Sefer Yetzirah, the Rav explains that everything exists in time, place and soul, with Yom Kippur, the Kodesh HaKodashim and the Kohen Gadol as the holiest of each. Talmidei chachamim are holy days among souls, like Shabbos on which no work is done, and ordinary Jews who support them are like the weekdays that are blessed through Shabbos; lesser talmidei chachamim match Yom Tov, Chol HaMoed and Rosh Chodesh.

title.en: Moshe Rabbeinu is a mo'ed

summary.en: The Rav explains that Shabbos and the festivals are called mo'ed, the Mishkan is the Ohel Mo'ed, and the talmid chacham too, since a mo'ed is where the Shechinah meets Israel. Moshe, the head of all talmidei chachamim and the 'Shabbos' among them, therefore camped before the Ohel Mo'ed; as each Jew's letter lies in the parsha of his own mitzvah, Moshe's private parsha is the moadim, which he taught in a special way.

title.en: The Torah as Moshe's eishes chayil

summary.en: The Rav explains that Moshe was wholly spiritual, a 'man of G-d' with no tie to the body, and therefore separated from his wife, as the episode of Miriam and Aharon shows. For him the eishes chayil of Mishlei meant only the Torah, his 'kallah'; every talmid chacham shares this in part, and Shabbos, when eishes chayil is sung, is that level. This was Moshe's da'as, which means full attachment.

title.en: Moshe's added day before Matan Torah

summary.en: Noting that this day is the first of the Shloshes Yemei Hagbalah, the Rav explains why Moshe added a day of separation: Moshe himself had separated since the desert of Sinai, and he wanted all Israel, at least at the original Matan Torah, to reach his level where the Torah is their eishes chayil. He urges using these days, and the last two nights of Sefirah, to sanctify oneself.

title.en: Preparing for Shavuos and its davening

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbi Mordechai of Lechovitch, who feared Shavuos more than Rosh Hashanah because on it one is judged on spiritual matters, and the Arizal that each Jew receives his portion of Torah at the reading and in Mussaf. The night is a mikveh of purity for the day's avodah; with the parable of an exhausted chassan and the Imrei Emes's ruling, he warns against staying up so late that one sleeps through davening and Akdamus.

catalogTitle: The Depth of the Perfection of the משפטי התורה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains, through the Zohar's teaching that Parshas Mishpatim holds the secret of gilgul, that every judgment of Hashem and of a Torah court is perfectly just, even when we cannot see the whole picture.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the laws of the Jewish servant and the Zohar's statement that the parsha holds the secret of gilgul: souls return to complete the mitzvos they left undone. A Baal Shem Tov story of a debtor reborn as a horse illustrates it. He explains why the Torah begins with the eved ivri: theft, which the Chiddushei HaRim sees in every sin, drops a Jew back to before the Exodus, yet Hashem never rejects him; the seventh year, like Shabbos, the inner point that cannot be extinguished, frees him for nothing. The amah ivriah shows Hashem searching for ways to redeem. A second Baal Shem Tov story shows that a seemingly unjust event settles an old wrong judgment. The world is conducted by the psak of Torah courts, as Reb Chaim Ozer's advice shows. Like those who blamed Mordechai or Yaakov, we do not see the whole picture; until Moshiach we hold on to emunah.

en: Following the Zohar, the Rav teaches that Parshas Mishpatim contains the secret of gilgul, and that the whole parsha speaks about the repair of souls.
Every person must complete all 613 mitzvos, corresponding to his limbs and sinews, in thought, speech and deed; what he leaves undone through his own fault brings him back in another gilgul.
Hashem never rejects a Jew: the eved ivri goes out in the seventh year and the amah ivriah even earlier, showing that Hashem creates ways for every soul to be redeemed.
Events that look unjust, even a verdict of an honest dayan, may be settling accounts from earlier gilgulim that we do not know.
The world is conducted according to the Torah and the psak of the Jewish dayanim, which is mirrored by the courts above.
People who blamed Mordechai, Yaakov Avinu or the gedolim did not see the whole picture; only when Moshiach comes will everyone understand, and until then one holds on to emunah.

Torah courts and the heavenly courts

title.en: The laws of the Jewish servant

summary.en: Tying the parsha to the end of Shovavim, the Rav goes through the opening pesukim on the Jewish servant: sold for theft, freed after six years, the gentile maidservant, and the ear piercing. He notes that the Rashbam reads 'forever' literally, unlike the Gemara, which says until Yovel.

title.en: The Zohar: the secret of gilgul

summary.en: The Rav brings the Zohar that the parsha holds the secret of gilgul, and explains that souls come down again to complete the 613 mitzvos in thought, speech and deed. One who could not do a mitzvah need not return if he learned about it; only his own negligence brings him back.

title.en: The Baal Shem Tov and the special horse

summary.en: The Rav tells the Baal Shem Tov's story, brought by the Chofetz Chaim in Ahavas Chesed, of a horse that was the gilgul of a dead debtor; when the Baal Shem Tov received and tore up the IOU, the horse dropped dead and the soul went up to Gan Eden.

title.en: Why the Torah opens with the eved ivri

summary.en: The Rav asks why the first laws after Matan Torah concern something as rare as a Jewish servant, and answers that the whole parsha is about the repair of souls. He explains that eating with a brachah repairs souls in food, brings the Chasam Sofer on the ox that killed a man, and shows how low the servant has fallen, since he may marry a gentile maidservant.

title.en: Theft: the root of every sin

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chiddushei HaRim that the Torah places the parsha of teshuvah and vidui by theft because every sin steals the faculties Hashem gave for His service. The thief sold as a servant falls back to the state of the Jews before the Exodus.

title.en: Shabbos, the point that cannot be extinguished

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem never rejects anyone and gave the Jews Shabbos: the dimensionless point inside the six sides, the spark in every Jew that brings him back. The seventh year frees the servant 'for nothing', a pardon like the torn IOU in the Baal Shem Tov story.

title.en: The amah ivriah and Hashem's ways of redemption

summary.en: The Rav turns to the Jewish maidservant, who can be redeemed in many ways and goes out at twelve even before the seventh year, as a symbol of Hashem searching for ways to redeem every soul. All suffering serves a tikkun, and when the time of the geulah comes Jews will go out free even if their tikkun is incomplete.

title.en: The talmid on the mountain

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Baal Shem Tov sent a talmid who asked about the Zohar to watch silently from a mountain: a rider loses his wallet, a second man takes it, and the rider beats an innocent pauper. The Baal Shem Tov explains that this settled a wrong verdict given by a careless dayan some sixty years earlier.

title.en: Never say the dayan was wrong

summary.en: From the story the Rav concludes that what seems unfair has a hidden reason, and brings the Chofetz Chaim's warning not to claim a dayan judged wrongly, since Hashem stands with honest dayanim. He adds what he heard from a great tzaddik: before Moshiach, old accounts were settled in the generation of the Holocaust.

title.en: Six million and the courts that run the world

summary.en: The Rav suggests that the six million correspond to the 600,000 letters of the Sefer Torah multiplied by ten, the completeness of Klal Yisrael. He brings 'mishpetei Hashem emes', explaining that the judgments look unjust only when seen separately, and that the world is conducted by what Jewish dayanim pasken.

title.en: Reb Chaim Ozer and the lung illness

summary.en: The Rav tells of a man with a hopeless lung illness who came to Reb Chaim Ozer Grodzinski in Vilna. Since that condition in an animal is disputed between the Beis Yosef and the Rema, Reb Chaim Ozer told him to move to Eretz Yisrael, where the Beis Yosef is followed, and he lived.

title.en: Jewish courts and the courts above

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that disputes belong before Jewish dayanim, not gentile courts, and the Chasam Sofer that each Jewish court has a court of holy malachim above it while a gentile court corresponds to the seventy heavenly princes. One who goes to a gentile court without permission is judged by those malachim.

title.en: We do not see the whole picture

summary.en: Approaching Adar, the Rav notes that Jews blamed Mordechai, and some blamed Yaakov for sending Yosef, because they did not see the whole story; so too those who blame the gedolim who told Jews not to go to America. Only when Moshiach comes will all be understood; until then one must hold on to emunah.

catalogTitle: הקשר בין מרגלים של יוסף' משה' ויהושע; ועבודתינו בימי הקיץ

oneLiner.en: The Rav connects the three episodes of spies in the Torah (Yosef's brothers, Moshe's spies and Yehoshua's spies) to the test of holy eyes in places and times of strong tumah, and draws from it the avodah of the months of Tamuz and Av.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Ohr HaChaim: the spies failed because they went as agents of the people rather than of Moshe, and he draws that every Jew is Hashem's agent and must stay bound to the Sender. He brings the Arizal that Yosef's words 'you are spies' meant the brothers' souls would later enter Moshe's spies. He then explains that Mitzrayim and Canaan are the places in the world most prone to immorality, which is why Yosef, the brothers and even Avraham were tested there, and why Eretz Yisrael's hidden holiness was covered by a thick klipah. Kalev, Yehoshua and Pinchas withstood the test with blessings, prayer and the merit of tzaddikim. The months of Tamuz and Av correspond to the two eyes, so their avodah is guarding the eyes, as the mitzvah of tzitzis teaches. He reviews the halachos of Even HaEzer 21 and closes with the greatness of guarding the bris, tied to Yosef, Shabbos and tefillah.

en: Every Jew is sent into the world as Hashem's agent, and succeeds only while he stays bound to the One who sent him.
The three episodes of spies (Yosef's brothers, Moshe's spies, Yehoshua's spies) share one inner theme: a mission through a land of strong tumah.
Mitzrayim, and later Canaan, are the places on earth most prone to immorality, and a place's atmosphere can overpower a person.
The greater the holiness hidden in a place, the thicker the klipah over it, so entering Eretz Yisrael required blessings, prayer and the merit of tzaddikim.
Tamuz and Av correspond to the two eyes; the spies' sin began in those days, and their avodah is guarding the eyes, as the mitzvah of tzitzis teaches.
Guarding the bris in thought, speech and deed is the foundation of the world and brings one to Shabbos, tefillah, yiras Shamayim and the kingship of Torah.

title.en: Agents of the people or of Moshe

summary.en: The Rav brings the contradiction between 'send for yourself' and the people's request in Devarim, and the Ohr HaChaim's answer that the spies failed because they went as agents of the people and not of Moshe. He concludes that every Jew is Hashem's agent and must stay bound to the Sender.

title.en: Yosef's 'you are spies' and the three spy episodes

summary.en: He brings the Arizal that Yosef's words to his brothers foretold that the souls of the shevatim would enter Moshe's spies to help them, and left them when their intent went wrong. This explains why 'the tribe of Yosef' is written by Menashe. He then lists the three times spies appear: Yosef's brothers, Moshe's spies and Yehoshua's spies.

title.en: Yishmael, Mitzrayim and the 'ervah of the earth'

summary.en: As an introduction the Rav explains that the seventy nations each have a midda in klipah, and brings R' Shimshon of Ostropoli that after the sar of Mitzrayim was killed, the sar of Yishmael took over Mitzrayim. Yishmael is the waste of Avraham's chesed, and in the world as one body Mitzrayim is the 'ervah of the earth', a place prone to immorality, which fits Yishmael.

title.en: Yosef's daily test in Mitzrayim

summary.en: Yosef, the height of holiness, was sent to Mitzrayim to be tested every day by Potiphar's wife, and the Rav retells the Midrash of his struggle. Hashem watches 'through the cracks' and helps when a person can no longer hold out; on the day of the great show Yosef stayed away, as a Jew does not go to theaters, and in that merit he was saved.

title.en: The power of a place: the Ba'al Shem Tov and Avraham in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav explains that a place's atmosphere can sway a person, bringing the Ba'al Shem Tov's wagon driver who suddenly wanted to kill him at a place soaked with murder. The brothers had to withstand Mitzrayim to redeem Yosef. He then reads Rashi's two explanations of Avraham's 'now I know you are beautiful' and shows how the second explains the first: the tumah of Mitzrayim overcame Avraham's usual guard.

title.en: Canaan, the spies and the fruit of the land

summary.en: Like Mitzrayim, Canaan was steeped in immorality, and Eretz Yisrael, the holiest land, is so sensitive that one who cannot guard himself falls lower there; this is what happened to the spies, who saw the 'nefilim'. The Rav reconciles two Midrashim on whether the spies took fruit: fruit eaten in holiness brings holiness, which was Kalev's advice, while the others took it only to slander the land.

title.en: Treasures buried under a thick klipah

summary.en: The Rav explains the Midrash that the Canaanites buried treasures in the land: with their sins they covered Eretz Yisrael's inner holiness, and only one who digs and toils finds it. The greater the hidden holiness, the thicker the klipah, so Yehoshua relied on Moshe's blessing and Kalev went to Chevron to ask the Avos to pray for him.

title.en: Yehoshua's spies and the months of Tamuz and Av

summary.en: The third spy episode: Yehoshua sent Kalev and Pinchas from Shittim, because both had already withstood such a test. The Rav says that just as there are places of great tests there are times, Tamuz and Av, which correspond to the two eyes, and since Shelach is read before Tamuz one must learn from it to be 'spies' of holiness and look only where one should.

title.en: Tzitzis, holy eyes and the advice for the summer

summary.en: The parsha opens with spying the land and ends with tzitzis, 'do not stray after your eyes'. Tzitzis means looking, like Hashem 'peering through the cracks', and it saved the student in the Gemara as Yaakov's image saved Yosef. Tamuz and Av must repair the spies' sin of the eyes, which destroyed the Beis HaMikdash; Kalev and Yehoshua, who did not fail, are the roots of Moshiach ben David and ben Yosef, and the advice is to pray, go to tzaddikim and connect to the root.

title.en: A Mitzrayim within Mitzrayim, and 'I am no chassid'

summary.en: The Rav applies Rashi's teaching that the Jews' dwelling place was the worst part of Mitzrayim: today too some places are worse than others. He warns against the yetzer hara's claim that guarding one's eyes is only for chassidim, and announces that he will read the halachos from Shulchan Aruch Even HaEzer, beginning with the Rambam's words on keeping far from women.

title.en: Reading the halachos of Even HaEzer 21

summary.en: The Rav goes through the halachos of Even HaEzer 21 on looking, closeness and touch, bringing the Gemara about Rabbi Akiva, the Mishnah Berurah's discussion of looking, the Gemara that one who shuts his eyes will dwell on high, the dispute of the Rambam and Ramban, the Shach, and the Gemara of the man whose illness the Sages would not allow to be cured by forbidden means. He stresses that these are halachos, not middos chassidus.

title.en: Shemiras habris: Yosef, the sixth, Shabbos and tefillah

summary.en: The world stands on guarding the bris in thought, speech and deed. The Rav brings that 'Bereishis' hints at 'He created the sixth', the midda of Yosef, which explains the importance of the sixth hakafah and the sixth aliyah and Yosef as sixth of the ushpizin; 'Tziyon' equals Yosef in gematria. Guarding the bris brings to kingship (Yosef, Boaz), to Shabbos, to the mikvah on erev Shabbos, to good tefillah and to yiras Shamayim.

title.en: The damage of pegam habris and the Chasam Sofer's student

summary.en: The Rav warns that Hashem punishes nothing as much as damaging the bris: one loses the tzelem Elokim and the connection to the truth of Torah, and even one's livelihood. He closes with a story from a student of the Chasam Sofer who confessed to his rebbe that he had looked where he should not, and concludes that one with holy eyes draws everything back to holiness and brings the Geulah.

catalogTitle: ביאור עמוק בענין שליחות המרגלים. שליחותינו בימי תמוז - שמירת עינים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the meraglim were tzaddikim sent to bring kedushah into a land of tumah and failed when they forgot whose shluchim they were, and that in Tammuz and Av every Jew is such a shaliach, called to guard his eyes and so help bring Moshiach.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the contrast between Bereishis and Shemos, where a tzaddik faces a rasha, and Bamidbar, where tzaddikim themselves fall: Korach, misled by his eye, and the meraglim, who set out on this very day, erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz. Following the Ohr HaChaim, they failed because they went as shluchim of the people rather than bound to Moshe and Hashem; every Jew is Hashem's shaliach and succeeds through bittul to the One who sent him. The Arizal teaches that the souls of the shevatim entered the meraglim to help them. The Rav traces three sets of meraglim: Yosef's brothers, Moshe's spies and Yehoshua's spies. Each was sent to plant kedushah in a land of tumah, as Yosef and Sarah did in Mitzrayim. Tammuz and Av correspond to the two eyes; our generation, facing unprecedented tests, must guard its eyes through Torah, tzitzis and tefillah, and may thereby bring Moshiach.

en: The parshiyos of Bamidbar teach that even tzaddikim can fall: the meraglim and Korach were great people who failed.
The meraglim failed because they went as shluchim of the people instead of nullifying themselves to Moshe and to Hashem who sent them.
Every Jew is a shaliach of Hashem in this world, and his success depends on how bound he is to the One who sent him.
Yosef's brothers, Moshe's spies and Yehoshua's spies were three sets of meraglim, each sent to bring kedushah into a land of tumah so that later Jews could withstand its tests.
Tammuz and Av correspond to the right and left eye, and the main avodah of these months is guarding the eyes.
Our generation lives at history's most important moment, and a young man who withstands today's tests over his Gemara can bring Moshiach.

candidateTopics: bringing kedushah into a place of tumah

title.en: When tzaddikim fall: Korach

summary.en: The Rav notes that in Bereishis and Shemos the Torah sets a tzaddik against a rasha, while in Bamidbar tzaddikim themselves fall. Korach was a great man who saw with ruach hakodesh, but as Rashi says, his eye misled him.

title.en: The day the meraglim set out

summary.en: The Rav points out that today, erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz, is the day the meraglim set out on their forty days. They were great men and tzaddikim, yet they fell, and the Rav says this warns that the summer is a time of danger in which even great souls can fail.

title.en: Sent by Moshe or by the people

summary.en: The Rav raises the contradiction between Devarim, where the people asked for spies, and Shelach, where Hashem told Moshe to send them, and brings the Ohr HaChaim that both are true. The meraglim failed because they did not nullify themselves to Moshe; since every person is Hashem's shaliach, success comes from staying bound to the Sender, which the Rambam says is the purpose of a hundred brachos a day.

title.en: The shevatim's souls within the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal that the souls of the shevatim came into the meraglim as an ibbur to help them, which explains why 'lemateh Yosef' is written by Menashe and not by Efraim, into whom Levi entered. The meraglim did not use this help, and so they failed at the most important moment of their lives.

title.en: Our generation at history's decisive moment

summary.en: The Rav compares a person's most important moment to history's: the time before Moshiach. He describes a world on the brink, held in the hands of a few men in the Kremlin, as in Tehillim 2, and says our small deeds and our blatt Gemara add what is missing, while tumah enters Jewish homes through radio, television and magazines, a test like that of the meraglim.

title.en: Greater tests, greater help

summary.en: The Rav says a young man who resists the yetzer hara over his Gemara may be dearer in Heaven than Rabbi Akiva's mesiras nefesh, because our tests are harder. The eyes that will see Hashem's kingship are those kept pure; as Yosef was helped by his father's image, Hashem sends today's Jew the souls of tzaddikim to help him.

title.en: Three sets of meraglim; the seventy nations

summary.en: The Rav lists three sets of meraglim in the Torah: Yosef's brothers, Moshe's spies and Yehoshua's spies, all teaching how to strengthen oneself in times of test. He then explains that the nations stand against the seven middos, that Yishmael is the kelipah of chesed and Esav of gevurah, and why Yishmael, a nation of immorality, came to rule Mitzrayim, the land of zenus.

title.en: Yosef's test in Mitzrayim

summary.en: The Rav retells from the Midrash how the wife of Potiphar tormented Yosef day after day and how he held firm without giving in at all. When his strength was spent, Hashem helped him with the image of his father, because Yosef had to bring kedushah into Mitzrayim so that later Jews could withstand its tests.

title.en: Leaving an imprint of kedushah

summary.en: The Rav tells how, about a hundred years earlier, Jews from America asked the Belzer Rav to come and order Jewish life there, and he declined, saying Europe had a thousand years of mesiras nefesh behind it and America did not. He brings the Midrash that Yosef and Sarah were taken to Mitzrayim to leave an imprint of kedushah, and explains that the brothers came there unknowingly, as the first meraglim.

title.en: Avraham's 'hinei na yadati'

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's two explanations of 'hinei na yadati' and asks how Avraham, who guarded his eyes all his life, suddenly noticed Sarah near Mitzrayim. He answers with Rashi's second explanation: they were coming to a land of zenus, and Hashem showed him that it requires extra strength. This is why Mitzrayim and Canaan are named together and why the Canaanim had to be driven out.

title.en: The meraglim's mission in Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that the meraglim were meant to do in Eretz Yisrael what Yosef's brothers did in Mitzrayim: bring kedushah into a land of tumah. Taking the fruit of the land draws in its holiness, and the Midrash about treasures hidden by the Canaanim means that the kedushah of Eretz Yisrael is buried and must be dug out with Torah, avodah and mesiras nefesh.

title.en: The third meraglim: Kalev and Pinchas

summary.en: The Rav explains that Yehoshua's spies, Kalev and Pinchas, faced the same test in the house of a zonah, and were chosen because they had already withstood tests, Pinchas in Shittim. He concludes that in every set of meraglim Hashem sends help, the souls of the shevatim or Yaakov's image, to one who wants to keep kedushah where it seems impossible.

title.en: Tammuz and Av: the two eyes

summary.en: The Rav explains that the forty days of the meraglim fall in Tammuz and Av, which the sefarim say correspond to the right and left eye, the eyes that wept at the Churban. The main work of these months is guarding the eyes, and this is why parshas tzitzis, with its looking at the holy tzitzis, comes at the end of Shelach; perhaps this is the last Tammuz and Av still to be repaired.

title.en: Turning Tammuz around

summary.en: The Rav brings Rabbi Shimshon of Ostropol on 'yemei bikurei anavim' and notes that Kalev of Yehudah and Yehoshua of Yosef, who did not fall, are the roots of the two Moshiachs. Following the Bnei Yissaschar, each month has a permutation of Hashem's Name; Tammuz's is entirely reversed and comes from Haman's words in Megillas Esther, and the avodah of the month is to turn it around, as in 'venahafoch hu'.

title.en: Guarding the eyes: Gemara and Rambam

summary.en: The Rav says Hashem sends us into a place like Yehoshua's spies' house of a zonah each time we go out. He brings the Gemara in Bava Basra and the Rashbam that one who could take another way yet passes a place of test is called a rasha even if he does not look, and the Rambam's advice that the best protection is to immerse oneself in Torah.

title.en: Tzitzis, tefillah and the shlichus

summary.en: The Rav explains Rashi's statement that tzitzis equals all the mitzvos: every mitzvah becomes part of the soul's garment, and tzitzis is itself a whole garment. He adds that one must daven as Kalev did at the graves of the Avos, keep good company, and above all never forget that one is Hashem's shaliach, since no one knows what the Torah will one day record about him.

title.en: Tonight's walk home is a shlichus too

summary.en: The Rav closes that tonight, the day the meraglim set out, going home to supper is also a shlichus whose purpose we do not know, like a businessman's trip. Those who pass these forty days will be written in golden letters, and with the travel season beginning he warns that travel must serve Hashem's purpose, and blesses that Tammuz and Av become months of seeing Hashem's return to Tziyon.

oneLiner.en: Speaking to children before the summer, the Rav teaches that every Jew is Hashem's shliach sent down to raise up the world, and that wherever one travels he must not forget why he was sent.

abstract.en: The Rav opens by telling the children that the Shechinah rests where children learn Torah. From the parsha of the spies he derives that every Jew is a shliach whom Hashem sends down to bring back Torah, mitzvos and good deeds; the spies failed, while Yehoshua's messengers in the haftarah succeeded through yiras shamayim and emunah. He explains that the spies' forty days ran from erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha b'Av, and that this is why everyone travels in these weeks: to rectify their trip by travelling as true shluchim, since every step is directed by Hashem. Every tree, stone and blade of grass waits for a Jew to make a bracha or learn there and so fulfil its purpose. Through the Chofetz Chaim's parable of the man who traded diamonds for tallow candles, he warns against forgetting the mission, and closes by urging the children to keep learning and davening in the country and to come to love and fear of Hashem through His creation.

en: Every Jew, down to every child who learns Torah, is a shliach of Hashem, sent from the heavens to this world to bring back Torah, mitzvos and good deeds.
The spies failed because they forgot they were shluchim of Hashem and of Moshe Rabbeinu, while Yehoshua's messengers succeeded because they went with yiras shamayim and emunah.
Wherever a person goes is decreed from Heaven; he travels for his own reasons, but Hashem sends him there to accomplish something in Torah and mitzvos.
Every part of creation waits to be rectified and raised up by a Jew who makes a bracha, learns or does a mitzvah with it.
On a summer trip one may look after his health, but the main thing is to behave with yiras shamayim, keep set times for learning and daven properly.

title.en: Every Jew is Hashem's shliach

summary.en: The Rav tells the children that the Shechinah is present where they learn Torah, then turns to the spies Moshe sent and says that every Jew is likewise sent by Hashem from the heavens to this world. He contrasts the spies, who failed, with Yehoshua's messengers in the haftarah, who succeeded through yiras shamayim and emunah.

title.en: Why everyone travels in Tammuz

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the spies left on erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz and returned on the night of Tisha b'Av, and asks why everyone packs and travels exactly at that time. He answers that Hashem sends Jews travelling in those forty days to rectify the spies' trip, which failed because they forgot they were shluchim, and that every step a person takes is directed from Heaven.

title.en: All of creation waits for a Jew

summary.en: The Rav explains that not only people but every part of creation needs rectifying: a tree waits thousands of years for a child to make a bracha on its apple, and a stone for a Jew to sit on it and learn. Wherever one comes was ordained by Hashem, and in davening one calls all creation to praise Him, as the Ba'al Shem Tov's sheep stood up and davened with him.

title.en: The Chofetz Chaim's parable of diamonds and candles

summary.en: The Rav tells the Chofetz Chaim's parable of a poor man who travelled to the dark mountains to gather diamonds, but there filled his bags with costly tallow candles instead. On the way home the candles rotted in the heat and had to be thrown into the sea, and only then did he remember why he had gone.

title.en: Remember your mission in the country

summary.en: The Rav applies the parable: souls are sent down to gather Torah and mitzvos, but people fill up on treats and arrive above with nothing. He tells the children to be good shluchim like Yehoshua's, to keep learning and davening on vacation, and to use the country's open view of Hashem's creation to come to love and fear of Him, as the Rambam teaches, ending with a wish for Moshiach.

catalogTitle: Insights into the ארבעה אבות נזיקין and the Significance of their Appearance in this Week's Parsha

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the four avos nezikin are the four forces of tumah opposite the four letters of Hashem's Name, and that a person's animal damages only because its owner's own traits flow into it, so guarding one's property begins with guarding oneself and asking Hashem to guard him.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Mishnah's four avos nezikin and links them to the four special parshiyos, which correspond to the four letters of Hashem's Name: Shekalim to the yud, Zachor to the hei, and after Purim wipes out Amalek, the vav and hei. Since there is tumah opposite kedushah, the four damagers are the destructive forces of the klipah, and Parshas Mishpatim, always Shabbos Shekalim in a plain year, begins the work of breaking them. He then asks why Rav learns that 'maveh' means a person from a passuk about teshuvah, and answers that a damaging man is not truly an 'adam', who resembles G-dliness; he regains that name only through teshuvah. A person's property is an extension of his soul, like a spouse, as shown by the heavenly voice before birth and Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey. So an animal's keren, shen and regel mirror its owner's anger, lust and bad habits, and guarding the animal means guarding oneself, ultimately by asking Hashem, the Shomer, to watch over him.

en: The four special parshiyos correspond to the four letters of Hashem's Name, and the Name is completed only after Purim wipes out Amalek.
The four avos nezikin are the four forces of tumah opposite the four letters, and Parshas Mishpatim, which is Shabbos Shekalim, begins the work of nullifying them.
A person who damages is not truly an 'adam'; he becomes one again only through teshuvah, which is why Rav proves that maveh is a person from a passuk about teshuvah.
A person's property is an extension of his soul, like his spouse, so his holiness or his faults flow into it.
Keren, shen and regel mirror the owner's anger, pursuit of pleasure and bad habits; one guards his animal by guarding himself.
Hashem is the Shomer of the world, and a person should ask Him every morning to guard him from sin and damage.

title.en: Four parshiyos, four letters, four damagers

summary.en: The Rav links the four special parshiyos to the four letters of Hashem's Name, explains why the Name is incomplete until Amalek is wiped out on Purim, and says the four avos nezikin are the matching forces of tumah that Parshas Mishpatim, always Shabbos Shekalim, begins to break.

title.en: A damager is not an adam

summary.en: The Rav says damaging is a sin that requires asking forgiveness, then asks why Rav learns that maveh means a person from a passuk about teshuvah. He answers that a man who damages is not an 'adam', who resembles G-dliness, but a beast like Yishmael, the 'pere adam', and regains the name adam only by doing teshuvah.

title.en: Property as an extension of the soul

summary.en: Asking why an owner is liable for his animal's damage, the Rav explains that a person's possessions are part of his soul, like his spouse: the heavenly voice before birth assigns him a wife, a house and a field, just as Chava was part of Adam. He tells how Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey would not eat untithed food, because the tzaddik's holiness extended into his animal.

title.en: Keren, shen and regel mirror the owner

summary.en: The Rav explains that an animal gores with intent to damage because its owner has a temper, eats for pleasure because its owner chases pleasure, and walks into damage by habit because its owner has bad habits. Hence the Mishnah's 'its guarding is on you' means a person guards his animal by guarding himself.

title.en: Hashem the Shomer, and blessing Adar

summary.en: From a Midrash on Kayin's answer 'Am I my brother's keeper?', the Rav explains that Hashem is the Shomer of the world, and a person should ask Him every morning to guard him from sin and damage. He closes by tying Mishpatim to Shabbos Shekalim and the blessing of the coming month of Adar.

catalogTitle: החוק של פרה אדומה - אהבת הקב"ה אלינו

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that the parah adumah is a chok because it rests on Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael, which is beyond reason, and that Moshe Rabbeinu's humility was itself a chok, which leads into the sin at Mei Merivah and the lesson of believing in oneself.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash that Hashem revealed the reason of the parah adumah to Moshe alone, so that all who perform it do so on Moshe's intention. He asks how the parah can atone for the golden calf and answers that a will has no reason: just as a mother's love for her child is beyond logic, Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael comes from the souls being a part of G-d. Moshe, who became one with the Torah, could sense this; Shlomo HaMelech sought it and found it far from him. The parah is also teshuvah through humbling oneself. Moshe's root was in anavah, and he explained his own greatness as a chok. Distinguishing leadership by gevurah from leadership by malchus, the Rav explains why Moshe hit the rock in Miriam's merit but was told to speak to it in his own merit, which clashed with his humility. He concludes that Chukas teaches belief in oneself, and applies it to the bochurim's task of instilling Yiddishkeit.

en: Hashem revealed the reason of the parah adumah only to Moshe, so that whoever performs it does so on Moshe's intention.
The parah is a chok because it rests on Hashem's will and love for Klal Yisrael, and a will has no reason, like a mother's love for her child.
Moshe Rabbeinu, who became one with the Torah itself, could sense the reason of the parah.
Moshe's root was in the mitzvah of humility, and he explained to himself his own greatness as a chok he could not understand.
Hitting the rock was leadership as the king's messenger in Miriam's merit; speaking to it was malchus in Moshe's own merit, which clashed with his humility.
Parshas Chukas teaches a person to believe in himself and in the hidden powers of his soul when he is placed in a position to do something for kedushah.

candidateTopics: chok and the limits of reason

title.en: Moshe alone was told the reason of the parah

summary.en: The Rav surveys the parsha and links the weeks of Tammuz to strengthening emunah. He brings the Midrash that Hashem revealed the reason of the parah adumah to Moshe alone, and explains that this way everyone who performs it does so on the intention of the tzaddik who understood it.

title.en: A will has no reason: Hashem's love

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi's mashal that the parah atones for the golden calf and asks how any offering can wipe away a sin entirely. He answers with the principle that a will has no reason, illustrated by a mother's love for her child, and explains that Hashem's love for Klal Yisrael is of this kind because every Jewish soul is a part of G-d.

title.en: Moshe became Torah; every Jew a palace

summary.en: The Rav explains that the root of the will is in heaven, and only Moshe, who became one with the Torah, could sense it; Shlomo HaMelech wished to become wisdom itself and found it far from him, while Doeg's Torah stayed outside him. He then explains Rashi's mashal: every Jew is the King's palace, a sin defiles it, and teshuvah through humbling oneself cleans it.

title.en: A chok demands humility; Moshe's greatness

summary.en: The Rav adds that a chok is understood only by doing it, bringing Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch on 'sechel tov l'chol oseihem', and that the parah demands humbling oneself, the opposite of the root of the golden calf. He asks how Moshe, the greatest man, could see himself as the lowest, and answers that Moshe treated his own greatness as a chok.

title.en: Moshe's root in the mitzvah of humility

summary.en: The Rav explains that every Jew has a root in a particular mitzvah, and that Moshe's root was in humility, which is bound up with the parah adumah. He then turns to Moshe's sin at Mei Merivah, noting that the meforshim, Rashi and the Ramban among them, struggle to define it, since Moshe was too great for us to grasp his sin.

title.en: Gevurah and malchus: two kinds of leadership

summary.en: The Rav asks why Moshe was told to hit the rock in Beshalach but to speak to it here, and how a chillul Hashem became a kiddush Hashem. He distinguishes leadership by gevurah, through strength and fear, from malchus, where people follow out of attachment, brings the Bnei Yissaschar on the Girgashi and malchus, and tells how a word of the Gerrer Rebbe was followed by many bochurim. A king's messenger carries the king's power.

title.en: The well in Miriam's merit; Moshe as a staff

summary.en: The Rav explains that the well came in Miriam's merit, so Moshe hit the rock as a messenger, like a policeman acting in the king's name. He asks why Moshe needed a staff for his miracles and answers by way of remez that Moshe saw himself as nothing more than a staff in Hashem's hand. After Miriam's death the water had to come in Moshe's own merit.

title.en: Speaking to the rock: a test beyond Moshe

summary.en: The Rav explains that malchus works through speech, as Moshiach will act through the breath of his lips, and that Hashem told Moshe to speak to the rock because the water now came in his own merit. This contradicted Moshe's humility, which saw no merit in himself, so it was a test beyond his powers, and the Rav says it was Hashem's plan that Moshe remain with his generation in the desert.

title.en: Believing in oneself; the parsha's flow to shirah

summary.en: The Rav shows a sequence of emunah: Shlach teaches emunah in Hashem, Korach emunah in the tzaddik, and Chukas emunah in oneself, including in one's own chiddushei Torah. He traces the parsha's order, from the chok of the parah through Miriam's death, Mei Merivah and the messengers to Edom, to the shirah, explaining that emunah leads to shirah, as at the Yam Suf and before the coming geulah.

title.en: The bochurim's task: engraving Torah in hearts

summary.en: The Rav applies the lesson to the bochurim of the beis medrash: like Yiftach, each must fulfill the role Hashem gave him and not say he is too small. Their task is to bring Yiddishkeit and warmth to children exposed to many influences, to be a living example, and to engrave Torah into Jewish hearts, as the word 'chukas' implies; he closes with a tefillah for kiddush Hashem.

catalogTitle: פרה אדומה - ביטול מלכות אדום; ביאור חטא מי מריבה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that parah adumah, the root of emunah that lies beyond understanding in every mitzvah, uproots the kingdom of Edom, and reads the sin of Mei Merivah as Moshe Rabbeinu's humility keeping him from acting by his own merit, teaching that a Jew must believe in Hashem, in the tzaddikim and in himself as Hashem's messenger.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a Midrash, brought by Rabbeinu Bachya, that parah adumah is connected to uprooting the kingdom of Edom. He explains that every mitzvah holds a point beyond understanding, and that this 'chok' of parah adumah flows into all of them. He then explains why Jews travel in Tammuz and Av: these are the days of the spies' journey, and travel with emunah rectifies their sin, since every trip is a mission from Hashem. A story of two Jews on the wrong train and Rashi on Hagar show that a believer never truly wanders. Following the Shem MiShmuel, the spies failed because they went as messengers of the people. On Mei Merivah, he explains that without Miriam's merit Moshe had to bring water by his own word like a king, but his humility did not allow it. From Shelach, Korach and Chukas he derives three kinds of emunah, and he closes with the hidden good of these months, using the summer for avodas Hashem, and blessings.

en: The Rav explains that every mitzvah contains a point beyond understanding, the 'chok' of parah adumah, which is why it is called 'the chok of the Torah'.
He explains that Jews travel in Tammuz and Av because these are the days of the spies' journey, and traveling with emunah rectifies their sin.
Every Jew is a messenger of Hashem, and success depends on remembering whose messenger one is.
The Rav explains Mei Merivah: without Miriam's merit Moshe had to bring water by his own word like a king, but his humility led him to strike the rock like a policeman.
He teaches three kinds of emunah: in Hashem (Shelach), in Moshe and the Sages (Korach), and in oneself (Chukas).
Tammuz and Av hold a great hidden good, covered over like an orlah, which a Jew as Hashem's messenger is to uncover.

candidateTopics: chok beyond understanding in every mitzvah

title.en: Parah adumah and the chok in every mitzvah

summary.en: The Rav opens with the Midrash, brought by Rabbeinu Bachya, connecting parah adumah to uprooting the kingdom of Edom. He then explains 'zos chukas haTorah': all mitzvos are bound together, and every mitzvah, even one we understand, carries a point of parah adumah that is beyond understanding.

title.en: Summer travel as a mission from Hashem

summary.en: The Rav explains that travel in Tammuz and Av rectifies the spies' journey, and that every trip is guided by hashgacha pratis for a purpose one may never know, citing the Ba'al Shem Tov. He tells of two Jews who took the wrong train in Russia, brings Rashi on Hagar's wandering, and concludes that a believing Jew never truly gets lost because every Jew is Hashem's messenger.

title.en: Whose messengers were the spies?

summary.en: The Rav brings the Shem MiShmuel's question of who sent the spies, Hashem through Moshe or the people, and his answer that the spies failed because they went as the people's messengers. He describes people rushing on 13th Avenue without knowing whose messengers they are, and contrasts the spies Moshe sent to Yazer, Calev and Pinchas according to Targum Yonasan, who succeeded because they knew who sent them.

title.en: Mei Merivah: king and policeman

summary.en: The Rav notes that the sin of Mei Merivah is hard to understand and that the Ohr HaChaim refutes many explanations. He explains with two kinds of authority, the king who rules by his word and the policeman who needs a stick: with Miriam's merit Moshe acted as an agent and struck the rock, but after her passing he had to command by his own merit, and his humility would not allow it. He then brings Rav Samson Raphael Hirsch on the link between Shelach and Korach as emunah in Hashem and in Moshe.

title.en: Emunah in oneself and the hidden light of Tammuz

summary.en: The Rav adds a third emunah taught by Chukas: believing in oneself, which Moshe lacked at the rock. He brings sefarim hakedoshim that Tammuz and Av are truly bright days of redemption, as Zechariah foretells, covered now by judgment because of the spies like an orlah, and says that Chukas begins the conquest of the land, when every Jew as Hashem's messenger can rectify his portion.

title.en: Using the summer, and parting blessings

summary.en: The Rav says the summer is not a time of license but a time to see Hashem's creation, citing the Rambam on coming to love Hashem through His works, and to gain strength for the year while knowing one is Hashem's messenger, thereby uprooting the kingdom of Edom through the power of parah adumah. He sums up that emunah is the root of the mitzvos, beyond understanding, in Hashem, in the Sages and in oneself, and closes with blessings for the vacation, citing the Gemara in Berachos.

catalogTitle: Doctrine של בלעם - “לא ראה עמל בישראל” - יהודי טוב בעצם

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains Bilam's 'doctrine' in Parshas Balak: the Jewish people stand apart from the nations, their good is their essence and their sins only incidental, and he shows it in the thirty-nine lashes, the Oral Torah and the meaning of Shiva Asar B'Tammuz.

abstract.en: Opening on the Shabbos before the Three Weeks, the Rav reads the navi Micha's call to remember Balak's counsel and Bilam's answer. Balak and Bilam argued that seventy nations should replace one; Bilam returned instead with a doctrine: the Jewish people dwell alone and are not counted among the nations, their good is essential and their sins incidental. Hashem had this said through Bilam, as the yetzer hara is made to answer amen. Through Bilam's three attempts and Rashi, the Rav shows that Hashem looks at the root, the Avos, where no Jew sinned. He applies this to the Gemara's thirty-nine lashes: the Oral Torah, flowing from the hearts of the chachamim, knows that the first day of a person's formation never sinned. The Mishkan may be destroyed, but the inner point remains. Shiva Asar B'Tammuz, the fortieth day, is therefore truly a consolation, to be seen with Shabbos eyes.

en: Bilam's doctrine is that the Jewish people are not counted among the nations: their good is their essence and their failings only incidental.
Even where the Jews seem to deserve a curse, Hashem does not curse them, because He looks at their root, the Avos.
Hashem does not look at the sins of Klal Yisrael, since a Jewish sin does not reach the root.
Every Jew has a point from the Avos that can never be blemished, however far he falls.
The Mishkan and Beis Hamikdash can be destroyed, but Klal Yisrael remains.
Shiva Asar B'Tammuz, seen with the eyes of the chachamim and of Shabbos, is a consolation for Klal Yisrael.

title.en: Before the Three Weeks: remember Balak's counsel

summary.en: The Rav opens on the Shabbos before the Three Weeks with the navi Micha's call to remember what Balak planned and what Bilam answered. He brings the Midrash that they argued seventy nations should serve Hashem instead of one, and that Bilam offered more korbanos than the Avos together.

title.en: Bilam's doctrine: a people that dwells alone

summary.en: The Rav explains 'hen am levadad yishkon' with a census in which dogs are not counted with people: the Jews are in another category entirely, their good essential and their sins incidental. He asks why Hashem gave this message through Bilam and answers that it is like the yetzer hara being made to answer amen.

title.en: No curse, for He looks at the root

summary.en: Through Bilam's first two prophecies and Rashi, the Rav shows that Hashem does not curse the Jews even when they seem to deserve it, because He looks at their root in the Avos, like a tree whose root testifies to its fruit. 'Lo hibit aven beYaakov' means that Hashem does not look at their sins.

title.en: Why only thirty-nine lashes?

summary.en: The Rav asks why Hashem disregards Jewish sins, and brings the Gemara that people who stand for a sefer Torah but not for a talmid chacham are foolish, since the chachamim reduced the Torah's forty lashes to thirty-nine. He then tells of a question that came up when he taught the curses of Ki Savo to young children.

title.en: Blessing belongs to the Oral Torah

summary.en: The Rav brings a child's answer: Hashem left the blessings to the Oral Torah, which is called kallah, the source of blessing, and is higher than the Written Torah, since the bris was made on it. He then brings the Midrash that the forty lashes correspond to the forty days of Torah or of a person's formation.

title.en: The first day of formation never sinned

summary.en: The Rav explains that the chachamim's thirty-nine follows from Bilam's doctrine: a Jewish sin is only incidental and never reaches the root from the Avos. The Oral Torah in their hearts knows that the first day of a Jew's formation, where the hidden love for Hashem lies, never sinned, so no lash corresponds to it.

title.en: The point that cannot be destroyed; Korach

summary.en: The Rav contrasts the forty written in the Chumash with the thirty-nine of the Oral Torah in the heart of the talmid chacham, and teaches that an inner point, in the soul as in the place of the Mikdash, can never be destroyed. He brings Rashi on why Yaakov is not named in Korach's lineage: even a blemish reaching to Levi cannot touch the point from the Avos.

title.en: Bilam's third attempt: the sin of the egel

summary.en: The Rav explains that Bilam's third attempt turned to the sin of the golden calf, the weapon accusers still use, as he was told the Arabs at the Kosel recall it. Hashem answered with 'mishkenosecha': the Mishkan would be destroyed instead of the people, and in the Holy of Holies, full of gold, there is no memory of sin.

title.en: Moshiach, and parah adumah as a chok

summary.en: The Rav says the answer to the destruction is Moshiach, the subject of Bilam's third prophecy, which ends with blessing. He brings the Kedushas Levi: the nations ask the reason of parah adumah to recall the egel, so Hashem answers that it is a chok.

title.en: The fortieth day: Shiva Asar B'Tammuz

summary.en: The Rav explains that Moshe's forty days began on the seventh of Sivan and ended on Shiva Asar B'Tammuz, the day the Oral Torah came down. Though the luchos were broken then, with the eyes of the chachamim it is the fortieth day for which no lash comes, a consolation, and he connects this to the Magen Avraham on the second day of Yom Tov.

title.en: Seeing the week with Shabbos eyes

summary.en: The Rav concludes that on Shiva Asar B'Tammuz itself one mourns and fasts, but on Shabbos Balak one looks with Shabbos eyes and sees the consolation. He calls to absorb Bilam's doctrine before the Three Weeks and to prepare for Shabbos with joy, drawing its blessing.

catalogTitle: Remembering the Forgotten Jew

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Moshe forgot what he made from the surplus silver because it came from the Jews outside the 600,000, the 'forgotten' ones, and that Rabbi Akiva, who expounds even the crowns on the letters, reconnects them, as Purim of the thirteenth month does.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the accounting of Pekudei: the half-shekels of 600,000 Jews became the hundred sockets, and the 1,775 surplus shekels became hooks for the pillars. Mocked by the scoffers of the generation, Moshe gave a full reckoning but forgot what he did with the surplus until, per the Megaleh Amukos, Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him. A long detour explains why the akeida was the great test: Hashem seemed distant and the promise seemed broken, and Avraham believed anyway. Following the Ramban's rule that the fathers' lives foreshadow their children's, the last test before Moshiach is the same, a generation of double concealment, the thirteenth month. The surplus donors are the Jews outside the camp, forgotten, so their silver was forgotten too and hung outside the curtains. Rabbi Akiva, who expounded the crowns on the letters, reconnects them; the hooks are vavim, connectors. Purim, in a thirteenth month this year, is the day for these Jews.

en: The silver of the half-shekels of 600,000 Jews became the hundred sockets on which the Mishkan stood; the 1,775 surplus shekels became the hooks of the pillars.
The akeida was the greatest test because Avraham had to believe while Hashem seemed distant and His promise seemed contradicted.
By the Ramban's rule that the fathers' lives are a sign for the children, the last test before Moshiach is the test of the akeida: believing when it is hard to believe.
The Jews beyond the 600,000 stand outside the Mishkan and are 'forgotten', so Moshe forgot what became of their silver.
Rabbi Akiva, who expounded the crowns on the letters, reconnects the rejected Jews to Klal Yisroel and reminded Moshe where their silver went.
Purim, falling this year in the thirteenth month, is the day for the Jews who seem outside; it reaches down to a Jew in his lowest state.
