Rabbi Akiva and the crowns of the letters
the akeida as a test of faith
emunah in the footsteps of Moshiach

title.en: The accounting of the Mishkan's silver

summary.en: The Rav reads the opening of Pekudei, notes that Betzalel of Yehudah was joined by Oholiav of Dan, and goes through the count of the silver: the half-shekels of 600,000 made a hundred sockets, and the 1,775 surplus shekels became hooks for the pillars.

title.en: The scoffers, and the silver Moshe forgot

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the scoffers of the generation said Moshe got rich from the donations, warns of the danger of ridicule, and tells how Moshe, giving a full accounting, forgot what he did with the surplus silver until, per the Megaleh Amukos, Rabbi Akiva's soul reminded him.

title.en: Eikev: the test of the last generation

summary.en: Going off on what he calls a tangent, the Rav reads 'v'haya eikev tishme'un' as the end of days, when everyone will listen, and as a joy reserved for the last generation, whose test is holding on to emunah in a world built on atheism; he tells of the Ba'al Shem Tov leaving a wagon driver who had no faith at all.

title.en: Why the akeida is called the test

summary.en: The Rav asks why only the akeida is called a test, contrasts it with Avraham's first test in Ur Kasdim, explains that nisayon means both test and raising up, and asks why the last test should be harder when the first, before Avraham had prophecy, seems the harder one.

title.en: Seeing Hashem from afar

summary.en: Answering from the Zohar, the Rav explains that at the akeida Hashem seemed distant: the command contradicted the promise of Yitzchak, and Avraham had to believe with questions he could not answer. He asks why Avraham did not see the angel's simple answer himself and answers that in a test Hashem closes even a wise man's eyes.

title.en: The akeida test of our generation

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ramban's rule that what happened to the fathers foretells the children, and concludes that the nation's last test before Moshiach is the akeida's test of believing amid questions, such as those after the Holocaust. Only Torah and mitzvos nourish emunah, and the answers will be clear when Moshiach comes, as in the Chazon Ish's parable of the tailor.

title.en: Double concealment and those outside the camp

summary.en: The Rav explains that the ten tests recur in place and time, that our generation is the double concealment of 'haster astir', the thirteenth month, and that there is a thirteenth group outside the tribes, expelled from the Clouds of Glory and exposed to Amalek. He then describes the Mishkan's holy courtyard and how the half-shekels of the 600,000 became the sockets on which it all rested.

title.en: The forgotten Jews and their hooks

summary.en: The Rav explains that the surplus Jews beyond the 600,000 were not worthy to be the sockets; their silver became hooks protruding outside the curtains, where the Shechinah does not rest. They are 'forgotten' because they forgot Hashem, so Moshe forgot their silver. The tzaddik connects them to the letters, like the crowns on the letters shin, ayin, tes, nun, zayin, gimel, tzadi.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva expounds the crowns

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara in Menachos where Moshe sees Rabbi Akiva expounding the crowns of the letters, and the Maharal's explanation: Moshe, the soul that includes all 600,000, holds to the body of the Torah, while Rabbi Akiva expounds the extensions. So Rabbi Akiva reaches the rejected Jews, connects them and neutralizes the Satan's hold, and he reminded Moshe that the surplus became vavim, connectors.

title.en: Purim in the thirteenth month

summary.en: The Rav explains that Purim, this year in a thirteenth month outside the twelve, is the day of the rejected, when many became Jews. He tells how Rabbi Yosef Chaim Sonnenfeld answered Rabbi Isser Zalman Meltzer about going to the mikveh, applies it to Purim, and explains drinking on Purim as showing that even in his lowest state a Jew is loved by Hashem.

catalogTitle: “על כן יאמרו המושלים באו חשבון” - השייכות בין הפשט והדרש

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows how the Gemara's reading of "al kein yomru hamoshlim bo'u cheshbon" as a call to make a spiritual reckoning grows out of the plain meaning about Bilam, and applies it to the fallen days of Tamuz, to strong communal tefillah and to a good chevra.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the passuk about Sichon conquering part of Moav. By plain meaning the moshlim are Bilam and Be'or, whose curse helped Sichon; the Gemara reads them as those who rule their yetzer and say, come, let us reckon the account of the world. Targum Yonasan brings this drash, so the Rav asks how it connects to the pshat. He describes Bilam's hatred of Israel, identifies him with Lavan, and shows that cursing Moav for money only let Israel later take that land: Bilam, ruled by his desires, could not see the future. The drash is therefore the lesson the Torah teaches through Bilam. The Rav applies it to the fallen days of Tamuz, the meraglim and Kalev's tefillah in Chevron, and the Ba'al Shem Tov's teiva of tefillah. With the Ramban and a letter on davening, he urges loud, united tefillah, a cheshbon for the end of days, and joining a good chevra.

en: By plain meaning the moshlim of the passuk are Bilam and Be'or, while the Gemara reads them as those who rule their yetzer and call for a reckoning of mitzvah against its loss and sin against its gain.

Bilam, overpowered by his desire for money, cursed Moav for Sichon without seeing that this would let Israel take the land; the drash grows out of this picture of a person who is not master of himself.
The days of Tamuz are fallen days in which the meraglim fell, yet Kalev and Yehoshua rose in them, and each year a person faces the same choice.
Following the Ramban and the angels' song, the Rav stresses davening aloud and together, with all voices joining into one.
Parshas Balak, read before the seventeenth of Tamuz, carries the power of turning curse into blessing, and the main place for that turning is tefillah in the beis haknesses.
Being close to a good chevra has effects that are felt even a thousand years later, as with the tribe of Yissachar camped near Moshe Rabbeinu.

teiva as the word of tefillah

title.en: Sichon, Moav and the two readings of the moshlim

summary.en: The Rav tells how Sichon took land from Moav so that Israel could take it from him, explains that by pshat the moshlim are Bilam and Be'or, and brings the Gemara's drash that they are those who rule their yetzer and call for a reckoning.

title.en: Targum Yonasan's question and Bilam's hatred

summary.en: The Rav notes that Targum Yonasan, whose drashos usually connect to the pshat, brings this drash, and asks what connection it has to Bilam. He then describes Bilam's deep hatred of Israel, comparing Balak's wish to drive them away with Bilam's wish to destroy them, and Bilam's belief that he could outsmart Hashem.

title.en: Bilam as Lavan and his foolish curse of Moav

summary.en: The Rav brings Targum Yonasan that Bilam was Lavan, and explains Bilam's wish to bless through Rivka's barrenness after Lavan's blessing. He then asks why Bilam, who knew the future, cursed Moav when this only let Israel take the land, and adds a Kabbalistic note that this land belongs to Keini, Kenizi and Kadmoni, where curses turn into blessings.

title.en: How the drash grows from the pshat

summary.en: The Rav explains that Bilam, who loved money and saw only the present, could not hold himself back; the Torah tells the story to show the shame of a person ruled by desire, and so the drash teaches that the moshlim b'yitzram live with a cheshbon, weighing the loss of a mitzvah against its reward.

title.en: The fallen days of Tamuz and the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav says the week of Chukas-Balak is suited for a cheshbon hanefesh. He describes the days of Tamuz as fallen days, when the meraglim made no cheshbon and fell, while Kalev and Yehoshua rose; the days will one day be turned to joy, and each year one faces the same choice.

title.en: Kalev in Chevron, the Nefilim and Og's teiva

summary.en: The Rav describes Kalev going to Chevron to daven at the graves of the Avos, then asks why the passuk mentions Achiman, Sheshai and Talmai. He explains that the Anakim descend from the Nefilim, fallen angels, and that Og survived the Flood by holding onto the teiva, which the Ba'al Shem Tov reads as the word of tefillah.

title.en: Holding onto the inner teiva

summary.en: The Rav explains that Og grasped only the outside of the teiva while Noach was inside davening and learning; seeing the Anakim showed Kalev how to hold on in a generation of Nefilim, by grasping the inner teiva, words of tefillah that shine like gems. He then speaks of this community as a holy place and a teiva in such a time.

title.en: The Ramban at the end of Bo: why we daven aloud

summary.en: The Rav learns the Ramban at the end of parshas Bo: the mezuzah and all mitzvos are reminders of the foundations of emunah, and the purpose of creation is that people thank Hashem. From here the Ramban explains why we raise our voices in shul and daven together, bringing the Yerushalmi on a strong voice and the people of Nineveh, and the Rav adds that we cry out so that we ourselves will hear.

title.en: Waking up: a letter on davening together

summary.en: The Rav warns that one can always find an opinion to excuse oneself, as with the Arizal's teaching on mikveh before Shabbos, but a seeker of Hashem knows which voice is the yetzer hara. Since everyone today is asleep, one must shout to wake oneself, and he reads a letter urging chassidim to daven together, word by word, aloud, neither too long nor too short.

title.en: Singing like the angels; turning curse to blessing

summary.en: The Rav brings the angels who sing with a great noise, all as one, and the Targum Yonasan on the song of the future, and describes the beauty of a whole congregation starting together. He then ties Parshas Balak, before the seventeenth of Tamuz, to turning curse into blessing, which happens mainly in tefillah, and urges effort in davening without fear of mockers.

title.en: Reb Zusha's hay and the time for a reckoning

summary.en: The Rav says a tzaddik weighs the future, not the present, and that today, near the end, every event is a hint from Heaven. He tells the story of Reb Zusha and the wagon driver's fallen hay, notes that computers allow great calculations as a sign to make an inventory, and speaks of the Shabbos that influences the seventeenth of Tamuz.

title.en: Tov latzaddik tov lishcheino: the power of a good chevra

summary.en: The Rav brings Rashi that Yissachar, camped near Moshe, produced two hundred heads of Sanhedrin, asks why this is remarkable, and answers that the passuk speaks of the time of the second Beis Hamikdash, a thousand years later. He concludes that one must join a good chevra, and blesses the listeners with a bright Shabbos and with curse turned to blessing.

catalogTitle: ביאור נפלא על מעשה זמרי וקנאת פנחס

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Zimri meant to bring the nations under the wings of the Shechinah but erred, while Pinchas was zealous for the indestructible point of Jewishness, the 'small yud', which is also the Kosel Maaravi that was never destroyed.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with a difficulty: Zimri was a prince of his tribe and a tzaddik, and Chazal say the angels sided with him against Pinchas. Drawing on the Megaleh Amukos, that Rabbi Akiva was Zimri's reincarnation and the wife of Turnus Rufus was Cozbi, and on the Arizal's explanation of Shlomo HaMelech's marriages to daughters of kings, he explains that Zimri wanted to bring the nations under the Shechinah. His flaw was a conversion not yet complete, and doing it before all of Israel, where the public would misunderstand. Pinchas was zealous for the point of Jewishness that can never be blemished but can be cut off through intermarriage, and was rewarded measure for measure. That point is the small yud of Pinchas and, in place, the Kosel Maaravi. Some truths, as Rav Ketina and Rabbi Yaakov Emden show, must be withheld from the public. He closes with the comfort of the Three Weeks.

en: Zimri was a great man and his act was meant for the sake of Heaven: like Shlomo HaMelech, he wanted to bring the nations under the wings of the Shechinah through a king's daughter.
Zimri's flaw was that Cozbi's conversion was not yet complete, a single hair of idolatry still on her, and that hair is the whole difference between a Jew and a gentile.
Every Jew has a point of G-dliness that no sin can blemish, but through a union with a gentile woman the seed of Israel can be cut off from its root, and for that point Pinchas was zealous.
Pinchas's rewards, living forever in his body and the kehunah gedolah, came measure for measure for guarding the Jewish body from mixing with foreign seed.
Some things, even when true and proper in themselves, may not be done or said before the masses, since others will misunderstand and be drawn after them.
The Kosel Maaravi is in place what the point of Jewishness is in the soul: it was never destroyed and the Shechinah never leaves it.

what may not be revealed to the public
Rabbi Yaakov Emden and the Zohar

title.en: Zimri's greatness and the angels' stand

summary.en: The Rav describes Zimri as the prince of the tribe of Shimon, appointed by Hashem and much older than Moshe and Aharon, and brings Chazal that the angels wanted to push Pinchas away. He asks what really happened there.

title.en: Rabbi Akiva, Turnus Rufus's wife and Shlomo HaMelech

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that Rabbi Akiva married the wife of Turnus Rufus, and the Megaleh Amukos that he was Zimri's reincarnation and she was Cozbi. He then brings the Arizal that Shlomo HaMelech married daughters of kings to bring the whole world to Hashem, and the Midrash that on the day he married Pharaoh's daughter the land of Rome began to form.

title.en: Pinchas's rewards and the point that cannot be soiled

summary.en: The Rav brings the Targum Yonasan that Pinchas became an angel who lives forever and will herald the redemption as Eliyahu, and the promise of eternal kehunah, and asks why his zealotry earned these. He explains that every Jew has a point of G-dliness that no sin can soil, citing the Shir HaYichud and the Midrash that Israel is like a nut.

title.en: Where the seed of Israel can be lost

summary.en: The Rav explains that one place the seed of Avraham can be cut off is a union with a gentile woman, since no Jewish soul joins that body. He connects this to the end of the zuhama at Sinai, and explains that Pinchas, who guarded the Jewish body from foreign seed, was rewarded measure for measure with eternal life in the body and with entry into the Holy of Holies.

title.en: Zimri's holy intention

summary.en: The Rav explains that Zimri's intention was the same as Shlomo HaMelech's: to convert a king's daughter of Midian and through her bring the whole nation under the wings of the Shechinah. He reads 'vayakrev el echav' as bringing her to his brothers, and explains that this is why the angels sided with Zimri.

title.en: The hair of idolatry and the tikkun through Rabbi Akiva

summary.en: The Rav explains Zimri's flaw: in his eagerness he did not see that Cozbi's conversion was complete, and the hair of her forelock showed idolatry still on her. Because he meant it for Heaven, he was reincarnated as Rabbi Akiva, himself a son of converts, and repaired it when the wife of Turnus Rufus converted properly.

title.en: The small yud and 'before all the congregation'

summary.en: The Rav explains that Pinchas saw the time had not come and was zealous for the point of Jewishness, which the small yud in his name represents. He then points to a second flaw from the passuk: Zimri acted 'before the eyes of all the congregation', where the masses would not understand his intention and others would copy him with base intentions.

title.en: The Kosel Maaravi as the point of Eretz Yisrael

summary.en: The Rav explains that Eretz Yisrael has a soul and a point no defilement can touch: the Even Shesiyah, which extends to the Kosel Maaravi, just as Avraham Avinu is the foundation stone of Israel. He brings the Midrash that Hashem did not let Titus destroy the Kosel, and notes that the masses cannot always be told such things.

title.en: Rav Ketina and the necromancer

summary.en: The Rav tells the Gemara in Berachos: a necromancer explained an earthquake as Hashem's tears over the Beis HaMikdash, and Rav Ketina called him a liar. The Gemara says the necromancer was right, but Rav Ketina spoke so that people would not be drawn after him, and the Rav learns that one must sometimes say such people are wrong.

title.en: Rabbi Yaakov Emden, the Zohar and the Shabbatean sect

summary.en: The Rav explains why Rabbi Yaakov Emden, fighting the sect of Shabsai Tzvi which built on Kabbalah, cast doubt on the Zohar's authenticity although all of Israel and the poskim accepted it and he himself cites it. He brings the Yam Shel Shlomo on giving one's life rather than deny even one halacha, and explains that to save Klal Yisrael one may have to deny a truth.

title.en: Nadav and Avihu, fire from heaven and the comfort

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yismach Moshe that the Beis HaMikdash was built for the sake of what remains after its destruction, the Kosel Maaravi, and the Zohar that the souls of Nadav and Avihu entered Pinchas. Their strange fire tried to hasten what must come as fire from heaven, and Pinchas repaired it. He closes that in the Three Weeks, the parsha of Eliyahu gives comfort: the Kosel and the point in every Jewish heart are never destroyed, and there one can pour out one's heart.

catalogTitle: Our נצחון over the .ארבע גליות The Center of the תורה is דרש דרש משה

oneLiner.en: The Rav shows how Parshas Shemini, read right after Pesach, is bound up with the days of Moshiach: the four non-kosher animals are the four exiles that will be overcome, the chazir will return to kashrus, and the middle of the Torah, 'darosh darash Moshe', stands over the se'ir of Rosh Chodesh Nissan that could have brought the final tikkun.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Acharon shel Pesach as the Pesach of the days of Moshiach, when the yetzer hara, represented by chametz, will be gone, and tells how the Sanzer Rav ate from everyone's knedlach on that day. He explains that the sedra is named Shemini because eight belongs to Moshiach. Matzah gives emunah, and the first Shabbos after Pesach the Torah warns not to damage it with forbidden foods, which clog the heart; he stresses how hard kashrus is today. The four animals with one sign are the four kingdoms; the chazir, Edom, will return to kashrus, symbolized by Ovadiah, a ger from Edom whose name matches the 91 pesukim of the sedra. With the Chasam Sofer he explains that the day of the Mishkan's inauguration could have been the tikkun, but Nadav and Avihu spoiled it and the se'ir of Rosh Chodesh was burnt. That se'ir stands at the middle of the Torah, 'darosh darash', just as Yerushalayim is the center of the world.

en: Acharon shel Pesach is the Pesach of the days of Moshiach, when the yetzer hara, which chametz represents, will no longer exist.
The mitzvah of emunah is to preserve the emunah every Jew already has, and forbidden foods clog the heart and damage it.
The four animals with only one sign of kashrus are the four kingdoms of exile, which change form like a cloud.
The chazir, which stands for Esav and Edom, is so called because it will return to kashrus when Moshiach comes, as the good part of Esav does teshuvah.
The day the Mishkan was inaugurated, Rosh Chodesh Nissan, could have been the tikkun of Adam HaRishon, but Nadav and Avihu spoiled it.
The middle of the Torah, 'darosh darash Moshe', is where the burnt se'ir of Rosh Chodesh is told, because just as Yerushalayim is the center of the world, that day was the center of time.

candidateTopics: Acharon shel Pesach and the days of Moshiach
Nadav and Avihu and the eighth day
Yerushalayim as the center of the world

title.en: Acharon shel Pesach and the end of chametz

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the peace of the days of Moshiach, explains that chametz is the yetzer hara and that a person's nefesh extends into his possessions, as with Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair's donkey, and says that Acharon shel Pesach is the Pesach of the future.

title.en: The Sanzer Rav's knedlach and fourteen days of Pesach

summary.en: The Rav tells how the Sanzer Rav ate from the knedlach of the whole town on Acharon shel Pesach, explains that in the future there will be a second set of seven days of Pesach which begins with Acharon shel Pesach, and mentions the harp of eight strings of the days of Moshiach.

title.en: The name Shemini, matzah and emunah

summary.en: The Rav explains that a name has meaning, so the name Shemini ties the sedra to Moshiach. Matzah is the food of emunah, and the mitzvah of emunah is to guard it from damage; forbidden foods clog the heart like cholesterol clogs the arteries.

title.en: Kashrus today and the Shabbos after Pesach

summary.en: The Rav describes how hard it is today to know what is kosher, with ingredients coming from endless companies, and says that on the first Shabbos after Pesach the Torah gives the laws of forbidden foods so as not to damage the emunah gained from the matzah.

title.en: The four animals and the four kingdoms

summary.en: The Rav brings the Midrash that the four animals with one sign are the four kingdoms, which appear as the four kings in Avraham's time and as the four kinds of nega'im next week. The chazir is Esav, who will return to kashrus, just as chametz becomes kosher by Shavuos.

title.en: Ovadiah, the ger from Edom

summary.en: The Rav explains that Ovadiah, a ger from Edom who became a navi, symbolizes the chazir returning to kashrus; his prophecy on the fall of Edom is like a forest cut down with axes whose handles came from it, and the Masorah's sign for the 91 pesukim of Shemini is the name Ovadiah.

title.en: The Chasam Sofer: the chazir after Nadav and Avihu

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer's explanation of why the parsha of the non-kosher animals follows Nadav and Avihu: the eighth day could have been the tikkun of Adam HaRishon, and only after it was spoiled did the Torah say the chazir is treif.

title.en: The burnt se'ir of Rosh Chodesh Nissan

summary.en: The Rav explains that the se'ir of Rosh Chodesh is the atonement for the diminishing of the moon; the very first one, on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, was burnt instead of eaten, so its atonement was not completed. Since the world was created in Nissan according to Rabbi Yehoshua, that day was the beginning of all beginnings and was meant to be the day of Moshiach.

title.en: The center in place, time and soul

summary.en: The Rav explains that Hashem created the world by looking into the Torah, and that creation began from Yerushalayim, the center of the world, like an embryo; in time the center is Rosh Chodesh Nissan, and in soul it is Adam HaRishon, whose soul is that of Moshiach. In the Mishkan in the desert all three came together, so that day could have been Moshiach.

title.en: Darosh darash: the middle of the Torah

summary.en: The Rav shows that the middle words of the Torah, 'darosh darash Moshe', stand over the se'ir of Rosh Chodesh, so all of the Torah's drashos flow from this center as Torah goes out from Tziyon. He contrasts Rabbi Eliezer's view that Bereishis is the center, points to the large vav of 'gachon' as the middle letter and the nachash's future tikkun, and closes with the need for a great yeshuah in the coming month of Iyar.

catalogTitle: י' זעירא של פנחס - אפילו 'איד'ן קטנים יכולים לעשות דברים גדולים

oneLiner.en: The Rav teaches from Pinchas, a 'small Jew' who rose to greatness when the great stood still, that in today's dangerous times every bochur in camp can be a Pinchas: by serving Hashem every moment, pulling others up, davening with fire, and teaching children with warmth.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with Pinchas, who earned an eternal covenant through his zealotry although he was then a simple, unregarded Jew; Hashem chose a moment when even the leaders stood helpless to show that greatness is not the monopoly of the great. Today, he says, is such a time: assimilation, collapsing standards and political danger call for individuals who stand up for kedushas Yisrael. He tells the bochurim in camp that the world was created to serve Hashem and that camp is a refuge for Torah, davening and middos, not for fun. With the Shem Sofer, the Toldos Yaakov Yosef and the Chiddushei HaRim he shows that the higher Jews either pull the simple ones up or are pulled down, a task for the masmidim toward the camp during the days of the meraglim. He then speaks of fervent davening, sinas chinam, tznius, and the greatness of a melamed who teaches by example and warms children's hearts.

en: Pinchas was a simple, unregarded Jew when he acted, and Hashem showed through him that small people can merit great things.
The Rav says today's danger to Klal Yisrael calls for individuals who stand up for kedushas Yisrael, at least in their own surroundings and home.
The world was created to serve Hashem, so every moment belongs to His service, and camp exists to grow in Torah, davening and middos.
The higher Jews either pull the simple ones up or are dragged down by them, so the masmidim must raise the camp.
How much fire a person feels in davening depends on how attached he is to holiness; one whose heart is sealed by worldly pleasure thinks the fervent are mad.
A melamed is like a star, small in people's eyes but truly great, and he teaches mainly by his own example and warmth.

candidateTopics: influence of the elite on the masses

title.en: Pinchas, a small Jew who rose to greatness

summary.en: The Rav opens with the pesukim of Pinchas's zealotry and reward, and compares him to shevet Levi, whose mesirus nefesh earned a reward for all generations. He stresses that Pinchas was then a simple, unregarded Jew, and that Hashem chose a time when even the leaders stood helpless to show that greatness is not the monopoly of the great.

title.en: A dangerous time that needs small Pinchases

summary.en: The Rav says today is also a time when small people can merit greatness, since the great have been taken from us. He describes assimilation, the decline even among observant Jews and the political danger to Klal Yisrael, like a candle beside a barrel of gunpowder, and calls for individuals who will stand up for kedushas Yisrael at least in their own home.

title.en: Why we came to camp: the world is for serving Hashem

summary.en: Speaking to the older bochurim, the Rav says it would be a pity to think one came to camp for fun and sports when Klal Yisrael is so dry of merits. Citing the Mesillas Yesharim and the Chovos HaLevavos, he explains that the world was created to serve Hashem and the soul came down to face tests, so every moment belongs to His service, unlike the outlook taken from gentile culture that gives G-d a portion and keeps the rest.

title.en: Camp as a refuge for avodas Hashem

summary.en: The Rav explains that in summer one can serve Hashem better in camp than in the city, whose temptations become unbearable then; as the Rambam advises fleeing to the desert, one came here to learn, daven and work on middos. Rest, sleep and exercise have their place as means to serve Hashem, but the purpose is Torah with upright chavrusos, better davening and ahavas chaverim.

title.en: Two camps: who pulls whom

summary.en: The Rav notes the two groups in camp, the masmidim and the regular camp of children from varied, sometimes very modern homes, and says Hashem put them together so the masmidim should influence them. He brings the Shem Sofer on 'Vayeshev Yisrael baShittim', the Toldos Yaakov Yosef in the name of R' Yisrael of Pistin on 'ki gamar chasid', and the Chiddushei HaRim on the meraglim: the higher Jews either pull the simple ones up or are dragged down, and the choice is now the masmidim's.

title.en: Rectifying the days of the meraglim

summary.en: The Rav says the forty days up to Tisha B'Av are the time of the meraglim, who were dragged down, and they are rectified by pulling others up; a mashpia, he explains, comes from 'shipua', a slope down which influence flows. He urges the bochurim to take from the roshei yeshiva and outstanding chaverim in camp, choosing the good, since bad influences will always exist.

title.en: Everyone can be a Pinchas, or a Zimri

summary.en: Returning to Pinchas, the Rav says that when few Jews learn or know they serve Hashem every moment, each person can be a Pinchas or, chas veshalom, a Zimri; the Torah is eternal and this week's parsha speaks to now. He adds that learning perek Yom HaKippurim, a perek of teshuvah, at this time is a good sign, recalling that the Chasam Sofer used to fast before beginning Chullin or Bava Kamma.

title.en: Davening: the Ba'al HaTanya's plea

summary.en: The Rav turns to tefillah, saying he showed in past years from sefarim how to daven with warmth, fervor and joy, and now repeats a passage from the Tanya, citing the Mesillas Yesharim on the value of review. The Ba'al HaTanya protests that one who davens at length should not be prevented, writes in the name of R' Chaim Vital that before Moshiach the main avodah is tefillah, and asks for lengthening in Ahavah Rabbah; the Rav concludes that tasting davening requires being immersed in Yiddishkeit.

title.en: The deaf man at the wedding

summary.en: The Rav tells of a modern wedding where all danced wildly to rock music he could not appreciate, and compares a deaf man who sees people jumping and thinks them mad. So one whose heart is sealed by worldly pleasure does not hear the song of creation in Perek Shirah and the angels' praise, and calls those who sway in davening crazy. He urges coming to davening on time so all begin together, as the angels praise in unison.

title.en: Sinas chinam and tznius

summary.en: The Rav says, from rabbanim who knew prewar Europe, that alongside its virtues there was jealousy, lashon hara and sinas chinam, which the Maharal links to Kamtza and Bar Kamtza and the churban; these days call for helping one another like limbs of one body. He then raises tznius among the masmidim, citing the Shulchan Aruch on dressing under a cover and the Gemara that Shaul was saved in the cave in the merit of his modesty, and asks the older masmidim to watch the younger.

title.en: The greatness of a melamed

summary.en: The Rav speaks of the worth of a melamed: a tradition from Lublin that if people knew it all would run to become melamdim, the Mitteler Rebbe drawing melamdim closer than rabbanim, and the Gemara that 'those who bring many to righteousness are like the stars' means teachers of children. Stars look tiny but are vast, and so is the melamed. All the masmidim are melamdim by their example, he adds, since a child who sees his rebbe fail concludes that Torah is lip service.

title.en: Warming children's hearts

summary.en: The Rav says a melamed can only give the warmth he has himself, and tells of R' Aharon of Karlin entering a cheder where the melamed taught Rashi on Lavan with feeling. Once mothers told children of Avraham Avinu and Daniel; today the rebbe must be father and mother too, and in camp, where the head is harder to reach, one enters the heart with stories of tzaddikim, the angels' song and the joy of Hallel. He closes wishing that the season be heartfelt and rectify the sin of the meraglim.

catalogTitle: צד א: בגורל תחלק הארץ - יהודי הוא גורל של הקב"ה - אנו גורלך ואתה גורלנו צד ב: התגלות הסוד שנגנז בימי המצרים

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that a Jew is Hashem's goral, bound to Him beyond reason, so he may not attach himself to the ways of the nations, and that the hidden good of the Three Weeks, revealed through the Arizal's teaching of sod, calls for strengthening one another and for tefilah.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Parshas Masei repeats the division of Eretz Yisroel by goral, already stated in Pinchas, and why it is placed between the command to drive out the inhabitants and the warning about those left behind. He explains that a goral expresses a bond beyond reason: Klal Yisroel is Hashem's goral, as on Yom Kippur and Purim, and an inheritance can never be cut off. Every nation stands under its own heavenly minister, and even its styles of dress come from there; therefore a Jew, Hashem's lot, must not dress, play or rejoice like the nations. In the second part he speaks of the Arizal, whose teaching revealed the hidden side of Torah and of history: the Three Weeks hide great good, and a broken person is great in sod. Comparing the generation to night swimmers who need a buddy, he urges mutual strengthening without envy, and stresses tefilah, which the Arizal said is the main pillar before Moshiach.

en: A goral shows a connection that cannot be explained by reason; Klal Yisroel is Hashem's goral and He is theirs.
Eretz Yisroel belongs to the Jews by goral, so those bound to it cannot keep company with the nations; hence the goral is placed between the verses about driving them out.
Each nation draws its ways, language and dress from its heavenly minister, so dressing like the nations belongs to the laws of avodah zarah.
A Jew eats, sleeps, plays and rejoices differently from a gentile; the wild shouting of the stadium is the 'kol anos' of avodah zarah.
Through the Arizal's teaching one learns that behind the plain sense of Torah and of events lies sod; the Three Weeks hide great good, and a struggling Jew is great in sod.
In the deep waters of the generation before Moshiach one needs a 'buddy': friends who strengthen each other without envy.
The Arizal taught that before Moshiach the world stands chiefly on tefilah, so one should come on time and daven together with the tzibbur.

the Arizal and the secrets of Torah
the hidden good of the Three Weeks

title.en: Why the goral is repeated in Masei

summary.en: The Rav reads the verses commanding the Jews to drive out the inhabitants of the land and to divide it by goral. He asks why the goral is repeated after Pinchas, and why it is placed between the two verses about driving out the nations.

title.en: Anu goralecha: a bond beyond reason

summary.en: Noting that Tammuz opens the last quarter of the year, the Rav turns to 'we are Your goral and You are our goral' from Yom Kippur. A goral, unlike a purchase, shows a bond beyond reason, as with Purim and the goats of Yom Kippur; he adds that an inheritance cannot be cut off, and that yerushah and horashah share one root.

title.en: The nations' angels and their clothing

summary.en: The Rav explains that the seventy nations each stand under a heavenly minister, and that a designer's new style reflects how his nation's angel is dressed. This is why the prohibition of dressing like the nations is in the laws of avodah zarah; he brings a story about the minister of Hungary wearing red, and the Shach on Esav's red garments.

title.en: Hashem's lot must not bow to the nations

summary.en: Since a Jew is Hashem's goral, the Rav says, he must not submit to the lots of the nations, each tied to its own land, language and avodah zarah; Eretz Yisroel is Hashem's land given by goral. He applies this to clothing worn for sports and brings the Gemara of an Amora who tore an immodest garment.

title.en: Kol anos: a Jew's joy is different

summary.en: From Moshe's words 'kol anos anochi shome'a' the Rav explains that wild shouting is the voice of avodah zarah, and that a Jew eats, sleeps, lives and rejoices differently from a gentile. He returns to the verses: because the land is Hashem's lot, the Jews must have no bond with the nations.

title.en: The Arizal and the hidden side of things

summary.en: The Rav says the Arizal's explanations often overturn the plain reading, as when he makes Korach a tzaddik, because his soul was rooted in the sod of the Torah. Just as Torah is full of secrets, so are the events of the world and of every Jew's day, as the Modim prayer speaks of daily hidden miracles.

title.en: The hidden good of the Three Weeks

summary.en: The Rav explains that under the din of the Three Weeks and the Nine Days great things happen in sod, and likewise a broken person who feels he is failing is great in sod. He speaks of the avodah of trust when nothing goes, notes that the Arizal passed away in the Nine Days, and urges using these days to toil despite their difficulty.

title.en: Night swimming and the need for a buddy

summary.en: The Rav describes night swimming where each swimmer must have a buddy, and asks why Dovid HaMelech in Tehillim cries out alone in deep waters. He answers that Dovid was a stranger to his people, and that a tzaddik passes trials so his followers need not; in the deep waters before Moshiach, as Malachi says of the yirei Hashem, one must join others and strengthen each other.

title.en: Without envy, and davening together

summary.en: The Rav adds 'nosnim reshus zeh lazeh': friends must not begrudge each other's success, and he brings the Eretz Tzvi on Kamtza and Bar Kamtza, that a son reveals his father's inner self. He then laments that people come late to davening here and urges that all begin and say the tefilah together, like many lights forming one torch.

title.en: Tefilah as the pillar before Moshiach

summary.en: The Rav brings the Arizal, cited in the Tanya from Rav Chaim Vital, that before Moshiach the world stands chiefly on tefilah, reading 'panah el tefilas ha'ar'ar' as written for the last generation. Bochurim must still give their full strength to Torah, but at davening each must add his share; he closes by honoring the Arizal and praying that the secrets of Torah and of the Three Weeks be revealed.

catalogTitle: תפלו על המן שהוא לבן - טעם מנהג לאכילת חלב ב9 טעג

oneLiner.en: Starting from the rebuke over the white mann, the Rav explains that the low days of Bein HaMetzarim, and the generation of the 'heel' before Moshiach, hide the greatest chesed, and that this generation's test is an Akeidah: serving Hashem with unanswered questions and strengthening one another.

abstract.en: The Rav asks why Moshe Rabbeinu's rebuke mentions that the mann was white. Every color comes from Heaven, and white is pure chesed; the mann fed Israel the way milk feeds a baby, without toil, so their complaint was against open chesed. Parshas Devarim falls in the Nine Days, when Jews eat milk to arouse the chesed hidden in these low days: where the kelipah is thickest the kedushah is greatest, and the Chasam Sofer says these days will become Yamim Tovim. Tisha B'Av is a moed, and its lesson is that Hashem is with the Jews in exile. History, too, has a Tisha B'Av: the generation of the heel before Moshiach, a time without feeling and of enormous tests. Its test is like the Akeidah, serving Hashem despite questions. Malachi's last counsel is that those who fear Hashem gather and strengthen one another, and Rus, which follows him, shows that destruction precedes the kingdom of David.

en: White is the color of pure chesed, and the mann, like a baby's milk, came to Israel through chesed alone, without toil.
Jews eat milk in the Nine Days because white foods arouse the chesed that lies hidden in these low days.
Where the kelipah is strongest, the kedushah behind it is greatest; the days of Bein HaMetzarim hold the greatest light of the year.
The generations form one body, and the generation of the heel before Moshiach is the Tisha B'Av of history: dark, without feeling, and full of great tests.
The Akeidah was Avraham's hardest test because he had to serve Hashem against questions he could not answer, and the last test of Klal Yisrael before Moshiach is of that kind.
Malachi's last counsel for the end of days is that those who fear Hashem should speak with and strengthen one another.

title.en: Why mention that the mann was white?

summary.en: The Rav opens with Chazal's reading of 'Lavan' in the first passuk of Devarim as the rebuke over their complaint against the mann, which was white, and asks what the mann's color has to do with the rebuke.

title.en: White is pure chesed: the mann as a baby's milk

summary.en: The Rav explains that every color comes from Heaven and white stands for pure chesed. A baby is fed with milk through chesed alone, without toil, and so were the Jews with the mann in the desert; their complaint was against food that came straight from Heaven.

title.en: Milk in the Nine Days and the hidden chesed

summary.en: Parshas Devarim always falls in the Nine Days, and the Rav explains the custom of eating milk then: white foods arouse the chesed hidden in these days. The days are low because great kedushah lies behind them, as the kelipah is thickest where the kedushah is greatest, and he brings the Chasam Sofer that these days will one day become Yamim Tovim.

title.en: Tisha B'Av as a moed: what to take away

summary.en: Moshiach is born on Tisha B'Av and it is called a moed, a festival still covered over. Just as one takes freedom from Pesach, Torah from Shavuos and simchah from Sukkos, the Rav says one takes from Tisha B'Av the comfort that Hashem mourns and sits with the Jews in their exile.

title.en: Acharis hayamim and the generation of the heel

summary.en: From the Tisha B'Av Torah reading, 'b'acharis hayamim', which the Chasam Sofer reads as Tisha B'Av, the lowest point of the year, the Rav moves to the generations. Like the year and the body, the generations form a shiur komah, from Moshe's generation at the head down to the heel before Moshiach, a part of the body that feels nothing.

title.en: The Tisha B'Av of history and the worth of a Jew today

summary.en: The Rav describes the enormous tests of ikvesa d'Meshicha, with the signs in the Gemara in Sotah, as the Tisha B'Av of history in which every accepted sanctuary of Torah, avodah and decency is destroyed, like an old building torn down before a new one is built. In such a time Jews must hold together, and the smallest good deed of a Jew today is immeasurably precious.

title.en: Why the Akeidah was Avraham's greatest test

summary.en: The Rav asks why the Akeidah is so great. A nisayon both tests and raises, and Avraham's ten tests grew ever harder. The first, being thrown into the fire for a Creator he had found through his own understanding, had no contradiction; at the Akeidah Hashem Himself told him to slaughter the son through whom the promise was to come, and Avraham closed his eyes to the questions and served Hashem without understanding.

title.en: The last test of Klal Yisrael is an Akeidah

summary.en: Using the Ramban's rule that what happened to the Avos is a sign for their children, the Rav concludes that the last test of Klal Yisrael before Moshiach resembles the Akeidah: serving Hashem with unanswered questions, as after the destruction of six million. Like Avraham HaIvri standing alone against the world, a Jew today must hold on to emunah, tznius and shemiras einayim.

title.en: Malachi's last counsel: those who fear Hashem speak together

summary.en: As there is an end of days, there is an end of prophecy: Malachi, the last navi, speaks in his last chapter to the last generation, which says serving Hashem is in vain. His answer is 'az nidberu yirei Hashem': those who fear Hashem gather and strengthen one another, remember the Torah of Moshe, and so cross the sea of heresy until Eliyahu comes.

title.en: After Malachi comes Megillas Rus

summary.en: The Rav notes that Tanach does not end with Malachi: in the Gemara's order the Kesuvim begin with Rus, and he asks what its message is. He touches on Chazal about the young women who spoke at length with Shaul because one kingdom may not overlap another, and on the rule that an old building is torn down before a new one is built.

title.en: Signs of destruction before the kingdom of David

summary.en: In the days of Rus the kingdom of David began to be built, so it opened with signs of destruction: 'the days when the judges were judged', chutzpah and breakdown, the same signs as ikvesa d'Meshicha. The Rav concludes that Moshiach is brought by the individual who stands apart from the crowd's chutzpah and follows Malachi's counsel, that those who fear Hashem help and strengthen one another.

catalogTitle: אליהו הנביא will Resolve the Difficulties in תורה by inspiring אידן to do תשובה

oneLiner.en: The Rav explains that Eliyahu HaNavi will resolve the difficulties in Torah because every kashya in Torah corresponds to a Jewish soul, and by answering it he brings that soul to teshuvah.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the Gemara on the verse in Yechezkel about kohanim not eating neveilah and treifah, which Rabbi Yochanan says Eliyahu will expound, and asks why mila opens Parshas Tazria among the tumos. He develops the theme of four klipos: the shells of a walnut, the four kingdoms, the four non-kosher animals, the four layers removed at a bris, and the four kinds of tzaraas, which Sefiras HaOmer comes to break. A bris is a miniature geulah, so Eliyahu, whose name he links by gematria to tzaraas, comes to it. Using the Ohr HaChaim, he teaches that a kashya is a klipah hiding a gem, and that every passage of Torah holds a Jewish soul: answering a kashya helps that Jew do teshuvah. This is why Eliyahu, of whom Teiku is said, will answer all kashyos. He ends with the Erev Rav, the Igra dePirka and Chodesh Iyar.

en: There are four klipos that separate a Jew from Hashem, and the theme recurs in the four kingdoms, the four non-kosher animals, the four layers of the orlah and the four kinds of tzaraas.
Tzaraas corresponds to Edom, which includes all the other kingdoms, so the Torah calls all four kinds of nega by the one name tzaraas.
Every bris mila is a miniature geulah, since it cuts away the four klipos, and therefore Eliyahu, the herald of the geulah, comes to it.
A kashya in Torah is a klipah that hides the truth; learning in depth breaks it and brings out the gem inside.
Every Jewish soul is rooted in a passage of the Torah, so answering a kashya in that passage helps the Jew rooted there to do teshuvah.
Eliyahu HaNavi will answer all the kashyos because he will bring all Jews to teshuvah, even the Erev Rav.

title.en: Mila in Tazria and the passage Eliyahu will expound

summary.en: The Rav asks why mila appears at the start of a parsha about tumos, and brings the Gemara on Yechezkel's verse that kohanim may not eat neveilah and treifah. Rabbi Yochanan says Eliyahu will expound it, while Ravina later answers it simply; the Rav says Rabbi Yochanan knew that answer but saw something deeper.

title.en: The four klipos and their many forms

summary.en: The Rav describes the four shells of a walnut around the four chambers that stand for the four letters of Hashem's Name, and shows the same four klipos in the four kingdoms, Avraham's war with the four kings, the four elements, the four non-kosher animals of Shemini, the four layers removed at a bris, and the four kinds of tzaraas.

title.en: Tzaraas includes all; Sefirah and Yechezkel's vision

summary.en: The Rav explains why the chazir gets its own verse and why tzaraas, like Edom, includes all four. Sefiras HaOmer is for breaking the four root middos that come from the four elements, and on Shavuos one reaches Hashem as Yechezkel broke through the four klipos in his vision.

title.en: Why Eliyahu comes to every bris

summary.en: The Rav gives a gematria linking the four negaim to Yechezkel's verse, then explains that every bris is a miniature geulah that cuts away the four klipos, so Eliyahu comes to it. Eliyahu, the malach habris, equals tzaraas in gematria, and mila overrides even tzaraas.

title.en: A kashya is a klipah hiding a diamond

summary.en: The Rav brings the Ohr HaChaim on 'Shmor veshamata' that a kashya in Torah is a klipah broken by learning lishmah. He explains that Hashem is present everywhere, even within the klipos, and compares a kashya to a hidden diamond that one must first locate and then extract; learning thus frees the sparks of holiness held captive.

title.en: Midrash peliah, souls in the Torah, and Teiku

summary.en: The Rav brings the Yismach Moshe about explaining a midrash peliah, such as the Midrash on Vayidom Aharon, and explains that every Jew is a letter in the Sefer Torah: answering a kashya in a passage helps the Jew rooted there do teshuvah. This is why Eliyahu, of whom Teiku is said, answers all kashyos, since he brings Jews to teshuvah; he adds a gematria of the four negaim.

title.en: Clarifying a halacha is greater than seeing Eliyahu

summary.en: The Rav brings the Igra dePirka that bringing out a halacha clearly is a greater merit than seeing Eliyahu, proven from the Gemara about Rabbi Evyasar: meeting Eliyahu would not prove his greatness, but Eliyahu's confirming his halacha did.

title.en: Eliyahu with a body and as a soul

summary.en: The Rav says there are levels in gilui Eliyahu. He brings the question how halachos could be learned from Eliyahu, as in the Gemara's seven teachings he said in two batei medrash, when Torah is not in heaven, and the answer that when Eliyahu comes in a body he is a link in the mesorah from Moshe Rabbeinu, but not when he comes as a soul alone.

title.en: Good Torah thoughts come from Eliyahu

summary.en: The Rav says every good piece of Torah comes from Eliyahu's power entering a person, and tells how Rabbi Yitzchak of Skver sent his son to see Eliyahu in the street, where he learned a lesson about parnassah from tied oxen. A good thought is Eliyahu using one's own body; behind every midrash peliah stands a neshama peliah, and Eliyahu HaNavi equals neshama peliah in gematria.

title.en: Neveilah and treifah: the Erev Rav

summary.en: Returning to Rabbi Yochanan, the Rav explains that beyond the four impure animals that oppress the Jews there are kosher animals that became neveilah and treifah: the Erev Rav, Jews who, as the Zohar says, will lead before Moshiach and are worse. Eliyahu will find their merit and bring them to teshuvah.

title.en: Grieving for Yerushalayim and Chodesh Iyar

summary.en: The Rav brings that one who has a kashya should pause and grieve over the churban Yerushalayim, since all Jews together are called Yerushalayim, and their teshuvah is its rebuilding. He links Eliyahu's seven teachings to Sefirah and to building Yerushalayim, and closes with the Bnei Yissaschar on Iyar as a month of Torah and tikkun.

catalogTitle: דרשה בירושלים עיה"ק - דרוש בענין הדביקות של הקב"ה בישראל שנתגלה בספר דברים

oneLiner.en: Starting from the halachah that the whole Torah must be written because it may not be written in scrolls, the Rav explains that the Torah and the world are a song made of connections, that the seams between the books reflect the exile, and that on Shabbos Chazon, when Sefer Devarim begins, it will be revealed that there was never a divorce between Hashem and Klal Yisrael.

abstract.en: The Rav opens with the parsha's crossing of the border of Bnei Esav, which he links to the days of Bein HaMetzarim. He then brings the Rambam that the mitzvah to write 'this song' means the whole Torah, since the Torah may not be written scroll by scroll, and the Chasam Sofer's reason: the drashos of smuchim connect each parsha to the next. Whole books may be written separately because no smuchim are learned between them. The Gemara calls the whole Torah a song, yet David was punished for calling it zemiros. The Rav explains that a song's sweetness lies in the connection between its parts, and that the world, created through the Torah, is such a song of seven notes completed by Shabbos. The four blank lines between the books, from which the get's twelve lines are learned, are the exile. When Moshiach comes it will be revealed that there was never a get, and Shabbos Chazon already carries that light.

en: According to the Rambam the mitzvah to write 'this song' is fulfilled only by writing the whole Torah, since the Torah may not be written scroll by scroll.
The Chasam Sofer explains that the Torah may not be written in separate parshiyos because the drashos of smuchim bind each parsha to the next; between whole books no smuchim are learned.
The sweetness of a song or niggun comes from the connection between its words or notes, not from each one alone, and this is the 'zemiros' David saw in the Torah.
Since Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, the world and all its events are also a song of smuchim, conducted by Hashem with order and harmony.
The four blank lines between the books, from which the twelve lines of a get are learned, mark the exile as a kind of divorce between Hashem and Klal Yisrael.
When Moshiach comes it will be revealed that there was never a get: the space between the books is the white of the Torah sheb'al peh, the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael.
Shabbos Chazon, when Devarim, the seventh book, begins, is the greatest Shabbos of the year, carrying the birth of Moshiach and a vision of the third Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: The border of Bnei Esav and Bein HaMetzarim

summary.en: The Rav opens with the parsha's pesukim about passing the border of Bnei Esav and explains that what exists in place also exists in time: the days of Bein HaMetzarim are that border, growing more intense toward Tisha b'Av. He announces the subject he will now speak about.

title.en: Why the whole Torah must be written

summary.en: The Rav brings the Rambam that the mitzvah to write 'this song' requires a whole Sefer Torah because the Torah may not be written scroll by scroll, the Gemara in Gittin and the Beis Yosef that whole chumashim may be written separately, and the Shaagas Aryeh's question why Sefer Devarim alone does not suffice. He then gives the Chasam Sofer's reason: the smuchim between the parshiyos would be lost.

title.en: No smuchim between the books

summary.en: Following the Chasam Sofer, the Rav explains that a whole chumash may be written alone because no smuchim are learned between one book and the next, connects this to Rebbi Yehuda, who darshens smuchim only in Mishneh Torah, and brings that the twelve lines of a get are learned from the four lines between the books, a sign of cutting off, while Devarim is not counted.

title.en: The whole Torah is called a song

summary.en: The Rav brings the Chasam Sofer in his drashos and the Gemara in Nedarim that the whole Torah is called a song, which the Rambam does not accept because of the Gemara in Sotah that David was punished for calling the Torah zemiros. He asks why that very verse is in Tehillim and said by every Jew.

title.en: The sweetness of song is in the connection

summary.en: The Rav explains what zemiros are: rhyming lines said a day apart or a niggun's notes played a minute apart give no pleasure, because the sweetness comes from the connection between them. He links this to the custom of music and rhymes at a wedding and explains that David meant that the Torah's smuchim give it such sweetness.

title.en: The world as a song of seven notes

summary.en: Since Hashem looked into the Torah and created the world, the Rav explains, the world and all its events are a song of smuchim led by Hashem as a conductor. Each day of creation added a note, and with Shabbos, the seventh, the octave is complete and the world can sing: Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos.

title.en: Seven books, and who hears the song

summary.en: The Rav brings the Gemara that the Torah has seven books, matching the seven notes of creation. Very few merit to see the song in history and in daily events; most people hear wild sounds and ask questions on Hashem's ways, such as why a tzaddik suffers.

title.en: Haazinu: the song of emunah

summary.en: The Rav asks why Haazinu, which seems to be rebuke, is read without arranging it to begin and end with good, and answers that Haazinu is emunah: it answers the questions on Hashem's justice and, as the Ramban writes, contains the plan of all history. He brings that one troubled by doubts should say Haazinu daily, and the Ba'al Shem Tov on seeing Hashem in everything.

title.en: All sevens are beloved: Shabbos, Eretz Yisrael, Kinneres

summary.en: The Rav brings the Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer that of seven days, lands and seas the seventh is beloved, and explains each as the completing note: Shabbos sings, Eretz Yisrael is the land that feels the song, and the Kinneres, named for the kinor, is the shaliach tzibbur of the seas. He tells of the Bluzhever and the Stoliner on one Shabbos.

title.en: When all questions will be answered

summary.en: The Rav describes the time when the world will understand Hashem's song and sing the Mizmor shir l'yom haShabbos: those who called the world chaos were fools, and the purpose was to show that Hashem is upright. Until Eliyahu answers all questions, the believer already sings both chesed and mishpat.

title.en: The seams between the books are the exile

summary.en: The Rav connects the letters of the Torah to the souls of Klal Yisrael, arranged like the camps in the desert; when they are joined the whole Torah is a song. In exile the books are separated by lines of kerisus: the expulsion is like Adam's banishment and like a get, which is why Maseches Gittin opens with a get from overseas. Only Haazinu remains a song on its own.

title.en: David, the soul of Moshiach, and changing halachah

summary.en: The Rav lists seven shepherds and explains that David, the seventh, completes the kinor and is the soul of Moshiach. When Moshiach comes the letters of the Torah will join together and one will darshen smuchim between the books, since halachah can change with the state of the generation, as he shows from Rebbi Eliezer and the Yismach Moshe.

title.en: David was right, but before his time

summary.en: The Rav explains that David, sensing the days of Moshiach, rightly called the whole Torah zemiros, but was punished for saying it before its time; therefore the Rambam paskens that today only Haazinu is the song. The Shaagas Aryeh's question remains a question until Eliyahu comes and the world sees that the whole Torah is a song.

title.en: There was never a get

summary.en: The Rav explains that the four lines between the books will remain, but in the future it will be revealed that they are not lines of kerisus: they are the white space of the Torah sheb'al peh, through which the covenant with Klal Yisrael was made. He brings the parable of the queen who waits for the king himself to raise her, and the passuk 'Where is your mother's bill of divorce?'

title.en: Shabbos Chazon and Sefer Devarim

summary.en: The Rav explains that on Shabbos Chazon, in the week of Tisha b'Av, Sefer Devarim begins: the seventh book, whose four lines are not counted for the get, the book of song and of Moshiach. He brings the Tiferes Shlomo that the Shabbosos of the Three Weeks are the greatest, and the Berditchever that on Shabbos Chazon every Jew is shown the third Beis HaMikdash.

title.en: A deeper churban in every generation

summary.en: The Rav explains that each generation in which the Beis HaMikdash is not built sees a new churban, as the sukkah of David keeps falling, felt most here in Yerushalayim, and asks how one can speak of song now. He answers with the light of Shabbos that already shines, the Bnei Yissaschar on Rebbi wishing to uproot Tisha b'Av that falls on Shabbos, and the weeping of the angels of peace.

title.en: The joy of Shabbos Chazon and the song to come

summary.en: The Rav closes: Shabbos Chazon is a great Shabbos, to be greeted with emunah in the third Beis HaMikdash. He brings the Avodas Yisrael that the Beis HaMikdash was hidden, not destroyed, says that every tear of the Three Weeks joins its building while on Shabbos a Jewish home is built with joy, and ends with the hope that Eliyahu will answer the question of the smuchim and all of history will join into one song.
